title_original: Sanlé Sory’s colour work comes to The Photographers’ Gallery
editorial_title_zh: 桑莱·索里的彩色摄影作品登陆摄影师画廊
editorial_excerpt_zh: 布基纳法索纪实摄影师桑莱·索里（Sanlé Sory）创作生涯后期的彩色作品正在伦敦摄影师画廊展出，为西非摄影呈现出更为广阔的视野
editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "heading", "text": "这位布基纳法索艺术家的后期作品揭示了西非摄影不断变化的时代精神与社会政治变迁", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "当被问及为什么摄影师画廊要展出布基纳法索工作室摄影师桑莱·索里的后期彩色作品——以及为什么是现在——策展人塔乌斯·达马尼（Taous Dahmani）的回答清晰而直接：“因为我现在在这里。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "她补充道：“我一直想把西非工作室摄影的长久传统视为一个全球性的平面。”达马尼厌倦了那些占据主导地位的解读，她认为，若要以更具生成性、修复性的方式理解这些照片，就必须对其功能进行重新定位。摄影师的工作具有政治性、艺术性，往往也带有论辩性和手势意味；但从根本上说，它也是一份工作。它是劳作。它是赚取报酬和生活的一种方式，不需要打卡，且拥有四处游历的自由。摄影是一段嫁接的历史、一段维持生计的历史、一段醒来去上班的历史。达马尼将目光从近年来那些被刻意放大、迎合西方艺术权力的“复兴”西非摄影展中移开，转而以其本来的面目看待它们：微小而私密。这就足够了。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "也许“纯艺术”——无论这意味着什么——是一个带毒的圣杯、一个带有活板门的基座、一座镀金的笼子。在这里，索里反倒是一位精湛的手艺人，但他寻求的是获得报酬，而不一定是去颠覆正统。纯艺术的这种诅咒，将索里的作品和个人风格固定为某种被发掘的事物，进而要求进行重新语境化和随后的拔高，这反过来又关闭了一扇通往现代世界的大门。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.1854.photography/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/SSc-0055.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "British Journal of Photography", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.1854.photography/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/SSc-0062.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "British Journal of Photography", "translated": true}, {"type": "quote", "text": "“［索里后期的彩色作品］在我们对西非创作历史的认知中带来了相当重大的转变”——策展人塔乌斯·达马尼", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "还原论式的解读往往将这类摄影师、乃至将摄影本身定位为一种历史事件，而非一个活生生的人。达马尼表示，这种局限的解读“拒绝进入当代性”，并将西方艺术叙事延续为“关于这段解放历史的可接受的乡愁形式，是对‘当我们解放了可怜的非洲人’那个时代的呼唤”。在大西洋的两端，以及深深的白盒子空间里，当我们看到西非的工作室肖像时，那总是革命的时代。一切从未改变，非洲就是非洲，西方就是西方。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "但索里的档案中保存着“成千上万”张后期的彩色底片，其中许多在最初的委托冲印之后从未被洗印过。达马尼发出了疑问，并试图将其引导至一种她所说的重新定位、“重新锚定”的方向。或许，这些彩色作品（这是对20世纪60年代和70年代早期黑白作品的推进）曾被认为更难为西方观众所消化，比我们所知（或被告知）的故事显得更不稳定。对达马尼而言，布基纳法索以及更广阔的非洲舞台并不是一个固定的事件，而是一个审视普遍摄影体系以及20世纪非洲历史特殊性的场所。“[索里的后期彩色作品]对我们所了解的西非摄影实践历史带来了相当重大的转变，”她说道。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "她将这种创作视为既普遍又独特的实践；它更贴近那些被定格在肖像中的功能性、政治和社会历史，并被理解为完全属于委约性质的人工制品。然而，通过在伦敦策划这场展览，人们也意识到家园并不总是一个能够回得去的地方，或许已经没有真正的语境天意留存。取而代之的是寻找新大陆、新生存与观看方式的可能性，这些方式将照片带给新老观众，但同时也允许所有旁观者亲眼去观察。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "西方艺术界对非洲的解读有一种倾向，即把非洲国家变成孤岛，将它们与周边同期发生的历史割裂开来。达马尼将此称为一种“被主导的、被恋物癖化的历史”，市场对此欣然接受，但这并没有让我们更接近于理解这些图像或这些人。她说：“对我而言，颜色成了出发点。我们能否通过色彩的镜头来批判性地思考这段历史？我们能否将它视作一种政治形式？我们所知道的大多数照片都来自1960和70年代。后殖民时期对抱负的追求、对快乐的追求……至少市场上是这么贩卖的。那些‘终于，非洲人民自由了！’的时刻。但它到此为止了。没有人去想后来发生了什么。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.1854.photography/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/SSc-0064.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "British Journal of Photography", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.1854.photography/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/SSc-0054.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "British Journal of Photography", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "索里后期拍摄的街头小贩肖像亲切而直接，这源于当时人们对委约肖像的需求逐渐减弱。拍照手机已经出现，时代正在改变。达马尼还强调了他受委托记录的后期拍摄对象们的愿望，并对他们对图像的投入做出了评论。“索里过去是用黑白胶片冲洗的，但当彩色变得更容易获取时，客户便开始要求彩色。它的成本更高，而他突然之间无法独自完成工作了。”在达马尼看来，被拍摄者和冲洗者都变成了生产者和合作者。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "达马尼通过历史上的迁徙追溯了被拍摄者的故事；你会时不时注意到某个为镜头精心装扮的人，“穿着一件稍微有点小、鞋子或许还没上油的西装”。通过这些图像，达马尼从时尚优先的解读转向了更接近融入社会背景的风格研究，即对二手衣和山寨名牌服饰的分析。这成了重新锚定的一部分，或许也是一种新型的非等级制摄影亲缘关系。它有助于理解普遍性，而非异国情调的特质，尽管这是一个同样深深植根于非洲的故事345345（此处保持原文数字与标点）。之深厚的非洲故事345345（此处保持原文数字与标点）。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "索里不得不与他的拍摄对象进行协商和讨价还价，因为归根结底，这些图像靠他们的支付才得以存在。他必须顺应潮流，跟上时代的变化。突然之间，人们不再想要他那著名的画底背景了。“他们想要成为新技术的一部分，成为被看见的新能力的一部分，”达马尼解释道。同许多西非肖像摄影师一样，索里很少在某种新兴当代的语境中被讨论。人们在策展上一直不被允许带着色彩、耐克（Nike）、奥巴马T恤和iPhone进入现代世界。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“我现在不再需要证明摄影是一种艺术形式了，”达马尼表示，“但我确实想回到这样一个事实：在历史上，有些事情我们太急于将其归入单一类别，而没有允许它们展现出多重属性。而且我认为，我们往往不允许非洲艺术家展现出多重属性。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "《Sanlé Sory: Colour Years》将于2026年10月14日至2027年2月21日在伦敦摄影师画廊（The Photographers’ Gallery）展出。配套画册由GOST出版，售价45英镑 https://gostbooks.com/products/volta-colour", "links": [{"text": "The Photographers’ Gallery", "url": "https://thephotographersgallery.org.uk/"}, {"text": "https://gostbooks.com/products/volta-colour", "url": "https://gostbooks.com/products/volta-colour"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.1854.photography/wp-content/uploads/2021/01/me-300x300.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "British Journal of Photography", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "艾萨克·赫克斯塔布（Isaac Huxtable）是一位出生于约克郡、常驻伦敦的作家兼策展人。他的工作横跨摄影媒介，核心聚焦于种族与现实主义。艾萨克目前担任维多利亚与阿尔伯特博物馆（Victoria and Albert Museum）的摄影助理策展人。他曾就读于考陶尔德艺术学院（Courtauld Institute of Art），随后曾在《英国摄影杂志》（British Journal of Photography）、摄影师画廊以及艺术机构Artiq任职。他的文字曾发表于《英国摄影杂志》、Elephant Magazine、Galerie Peter Sillem、摄影师画廊以及南伦敦画廊（The South London Gallery）。他尤其对纪实实践、性别、阶级和身体感兴趣。", "translated": true}]
article_blocks_json: [{"type": "heading", "text": "The Burkina Faso artist’s later work reveals the changing ethos and sociopolitical shifts in West African photography"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "When asked why The Photographers’ Gallery is displaying later colour works by the Burkinabe studio photographer Sanlé Sory – and why now – TPG curator Taous Dahmani’s answer is clear and direct: “Because I’m here now.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“I had always wanted to think about the long tradition of West African studio photography as a global surface,” she adds. Fed up with dominant readings, Dahmani argues that these photographs require a relocation of function if they are to be understood in more generative, restorative ways. The job of photographer is political, artistic, often polemic and gestural; it is also, fundamentally, a job. It is labour. It is a means to get paid and a way to live one’s life, void of a punch card and with freedom to roam. Photography is a history of grafting, of making ends meet, of waking up and going to work. Dahmani looks away from the recent landscape of “revived” West African photographic exhibitions, literally blown up for the Western art powers that be, and instead sees them as they are: small and intimate. And that is enough."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Perhaps ‘fine art’ – whatever that means – is a poisoned chalice, a trapdoored pedestal, a gilded cage. Instead, Sory is here a master craftsman, but one looking to get paid rather than necessarily disrupt the canon. This curse of fine art, which fixes Sory’s oeuvre and character into something discovered, demanding recontextualisation, and subsequent elevation, in turn shuts a door into the modern world."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.1854.photography/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/SSc-0055.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "British Journal of Photography"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.1854.photography/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/SSc-0062.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "British Journal of Photography"}, {"type": "quote", "text": "“[Sory’s later colour work] holds quite a significant shift in what we know about the history of West African practice” – Taous Dahmani, curator"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Reductive readings often position this sort of photographer, and by extent photography, as a historical event over a living being. Dahmani says this limited reading “refuses entry into contemporality”, and perpetuates Western art narratives as “acceptable forms of nostalgia about this past of liberation, a call to the time ‘when we liberated poor Africans’”. On the two far sides of the Atlantic, and deep in the white cube, when we see West African studio portraits, it is always revolutionary times. Nothing ever changes, Africa is Africa, and the West is the West."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "But Sory’s archive holds “thousands and thousands” of later colour negatives, many of which have never been printed beyond their original commission. Dahmani asks why and steers towards a relocation, a “re-anchoring” in her terms. Perhaps these colour works, a move on from the earlier black-and-white work of the 1960s and 70s, were deemed harder to digest for Western audiences, something less fixed than the story we know (or have been told). To Dahmani, Burkina Faso, and the wider African stage, is not a fixed event but a site to examine universal photographic systems, alongside the specificities of 20th-century African histories. “[Sory’s later colour work] holds quite a significant shift in what we know about the history of West African practice,” she says."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "She reads the practice as both ubiquitous and unique; closer to the functional, political and social histories caught within the portraits, and understood as wholly commissioned artefacts. Yet by curating the show in London there is an awareness that home is not always a place one can return to, that there is perhaps no true contextual providence left. Instead there is a possibility to seek out new lands, ways of being and seeing, ones which bring the photographs to audiences new and old, but allow all those looking to see for themselves."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The Western art reading has a tendency to turn African nations into islands, dislocating them from neighbouring, concurrent histories. Dahmani refers to this as a “dictated, fetishised history”, one the market embraces with ease but which brings us no closer to understanding these images or people. “For me, colour became the starting point,” she says. “Can we think critically about this history through the lens of colour? Can we think of it as a form of politics? Most of the pictures we know are from the 1960s and 70s. Postcolonial moments of aspiration, of joy… at least that’s how it’s sold. Moments of ‘Finally, the freedom of the African people!’ But it stops there. No one wonders what happens after.”"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.1854.photography/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/SSc-0064.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "British Journal of Photography"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.1854.photography/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/SSc-0054.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "British Journal of Photography"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Sory’s later portraits of street vendors, personable and direct, grew out of a slowing appetite for commissioned portraits. Cameraphones had arrived and times were changing. Dahmani also stresses the desires of the later sitters he was commissioned to record, commenting on their input into the images. “Sory printed in black-and-white, but when colour became more accessible, clients asked for it. It was more expensive, and he suddenly couldn’t work alone.” For Dahmani, both sitter and printer become producer and collaborator."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Dahmani traces stories of the sitters through historical relocations; every now and then you notice someone dressed fancifully for the camera, who is “wearing a suit slightly too small, their shoes maybe unvarnished”. Through these images Dahmani moves away from a fashion-first reading towards something more akin to socially informed style studies, an analysis of hand-me-downs and counterfeit designerwear. This becomes part of the re-anchoring, and perhaps a new type of non-hierarchical photographic kinship. It aids an understanding of universality, not exotic idiosyncrasy, though a story that is also deeply African."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Sory had to negotiate and barter with his subjects, as ultimately the images existed off their payments. He had to follow trends, keep up with the changing times. Suddenly people did not want his famed illustrated backdrops any longer. “They wanted to be part of a new technology, and a new capacity of being seen,” Dahmani explains. Sory, as with many West African portraitists, is rarely discussed within the contexts of an emerging contemporary. Entry into the modern world, with colour, Nike, Obama T-shirts, and iPhones, has not been curatorially permitted."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“I now don’t have to prove that photography is an art form,” Dahmani states. “But I do want to get back to the fact that actually, historically, there were things that we were too quick to put into one category, instead of allowing them to be a multiplicity of things. And I don’t think we often allow African artists to be a multiplicity of things.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Sanlé Sory: Colour Years is at The Photographers’ Gallery , London, from 14 October 2026 to 21 February 2027. The accompanying book is published by GOST, priced £45 https://gostbooks.com/products/volta-colour", "links": [{"text": "The Photographers’ Gallery", "url": "https://thephotographersgallery.org.uk/"}, {"text": "https://gostbooks.com/products/volta-colour", "url": "https://gostbooks.com/products/volta-colour"}]}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.1854.photography/wp-content/uploads/2021/01/me-300x300.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "British Journal of Photography"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Isaac Huxtable is a Yorkshire-born, London-based writer and curator. He works across the photographic medium with a central focus on race and realism. Isaac is currently an Assistant Curator in Photography at the Victoria and Albert Museum. He studied at the Courtauld Institute of Art, followed by roles at the British Journal of Photography, the Photographers' Gallery, and the art agency Artiq. His words have featured in the British Journal of Photography, Elephant Magazine, Galerie Peter Sillem, The Photographers' Gallery, and The South London Gallery. article_text:
The Burkina Faso artist’s later work reveals the changing ethos and sociopolitical shifts in West African photography

When asked why The Photographers’ Gallery is displaying later colour works by the Burkinabe studio photographer Sanlé Sory – and why now – TPG curator Taous Dahmani’s answer is clear and direct: “Because I’m here now.”

“I had always wanted to think about the long tradition of West African studio photography as a global surface,” she adds. Fed up with dominant readings, Dahmani argues that these photographs require a relocation of function if they are to be understood in more generative, restorative ways. The job of photographer is political, artistic, often polemic and gestural; it is also, fundamentally, a job. It is labour. It is a means to get paid and a way to live one’s life, void of a punch card and with freedom to roam. Photography is a history of grafting, of making ends meet, of waking up and going to work. Dahmani looks away from the recent landscape of “revived” West African photographic exhibitions, literally blown up for the Western art powers that be, and instead sees them as they are: small and intimate. And that is enough.

Perhaps ‘fine art’ – whatever that means – is a poisoned chalice, a trapdoored pedestal, a gilded cage. Instead, Sory is here a master craftsman, but one looking to get paid rather than necessarily disrupt the canon. This curse of fine art, which fixes Sory’s oeuvre and character into something discovered, demanding recontextualisation, and subsequent elevation, in turn shuts a door into the modern world.

“[Sory’s later colour work] holds quite a significant shift in what we know about the history of West African practice” – Taous Dahmani, curator

Reductive readings often position this sort of photographer, and by extent photography, as a historical event over a living being. Dahmani says this limited reading “refuses entry into contemporality”, and perpetuates Western art narratives as “acceptable forms of nostalgia about this past of liberation, a call to the time ‘when we liberated poor Africans’”. On the two far sides of the Atlantic, and deep in the white cube, when we see West African studio portraits, it is always revolutionary times. Nothing ever changes, Africa is Africa, and the West is the West.

But Sory’s archive holds “thousands and thousands” of later colour negatives, many of which have never been printed beyond their original commission. Dahmani asks why and steers towards a relocation, a “re-anchoring” in her terms. Perhaps these colour works, a move on from the earlier black-and-white work of the 1960s and 70s, were deemed harder to digest for Western audiences, something less fixed than the story we know (or have been told). To Dahmani, Burkina Faso, and the wider African stage, is not a fixed event but a site to examine universal photographic systems, alongside the specificities of 20th-century African histories. “[Sory’s later colour work] holds quite a significant shift in what we know about the history of West African practice,” she says.

She reads the practice as both ubiquitous and unique; closer to the functional, political and social histories caught within the portraits, and understood as wholly commissioned artefacts. Yet by curating the show in London there is an awareness that home is not always a place one can return to, that there is perhaps no true contextual providence left. Instead there is a possibility to seek out new lands, ways of being and seeing, ones which bring the photographs to audiences new and old, but allow all those looking to see for themselves.

The Western art reading has a tendency to turn African nations into islands, dislocating them from neighbouring, concurrent histories. Dahmani refers to this as a “dictated, fetishised history”, one the market embraces with ease but which brings us no closer to understanding these images or people. “For me, colour became the starting point,” she says. “Can we think critically about this history through the lens of colour? Can we think of it as a form of politics? Most of the pictures we know are from the 1960s and 70s. Postcolonial moments of aspiration, of joy… at least that’s how it’s sold. Moments of ‘Finally, the freedom of the African people!’ But it stops there. No one wonders what happens after.”

Sory’s later portraits of street vendors, personable and direct, grew out of a slowing appetite for commissioned portraits. Cameraphones had arrived and times were changing. Dahmani also stresses the desires of the later sitters he was commissioned to record, commenting on their input into the images. “Sory printed in black-and-white, but when colour became more accessible, clients asked for it. It was more expensive, and he suddenly couldn’t work alone.” For Dahmani, both sitter and printer become producer and collaborator.

Dahmani traces stories of the sitters through historical relocations; every now and then you notice someone dressed fancifully for the camera, who is “wearing a suit slightly too small, their shoes maybe unvarnished”. Through these images Dahmani moves away from a fashion-first reading towards something more akin to socially informed style studies, an analysis of hand-me-downs and counterfeit designerwear. This becomes part of the re-anchoring, and perhaps a new type of non-hierarchical photographic kinship. It aids an understanding of universality, not exotic idiosyncrasy, though a story that is also deeply African.

Sory had to negotiate and barter with his subjects, as ultimately the images existed off their payments. He had to follow trends, keep up with the changing times. Suddenly people did not want his famed illustrated backdrops any longer. “They wanted to be part of a new technology, and a new capacity of being seen,” Dahmani explains. Sory, as with many West African portraitists, is rarely discussed within the contexts of an emerging contemporary. Entry into the modern world, with colour, Nike, Obama T-shirts, and iPhones, has not been curatorially permitted.

“I now don’t have to prove that photography is an art form,” Dahmani states. “But I do want to get back to the fact that actually, historically, there were things that we were too quick to put into one category, instead of allowing them to be a multiplicity of things. And I don’t think we often allow African artists to be a multiplicity of things.”

Sanlé Sory: Colour Years is at The Photographers’ Gallery , London, from 14 October 2026 to 21 February 2027. The accompanying book is published by GOST, priced £45 https://gostbooks.com/products/volta-colour

Isaac Huxtable is a Yorkshire-born, London-based writer and curator. He works across the photographic medium with a central focus on race and realism. Isaac is currently an Assistant Curator in Photography at the Victoria and Albert Museum. He studied at the Courtauld Institute of Art, followed by roles at the British Journal of Photography, the Photographers' Gallery, and the art agency Artiq. His words have featured in the British Journal of Photography, Elephant Magazine, Galerie Peter Sillem, The Photographers' Gallery, and The South London Gallery. He is particularly interested in documentary practices, gender, class, and the body.

article_text:
横浜港⼭下ふ頭 の「THE MOVEUM YOKOHAMA by TOYOTA GROUP」 (以下、「ザ・ムービアム ヨコハマ」)で10⽉24⽇に開幕するシアタープログラム 「印象派モネと浮世絵 ［モネを魅了した、⽇本の美］」のプレス内覧が22日に行われました。広い会場を存分に生かして、印象派と浮世絵の世界が重なり合う色鮮やかなイマーシブ空間は、さらなる深みを増していました。

印象派モネと浮世絵 ［モネ を魅了した、⽇本の美］

会場：THE MOVEUM YOKOHAMA by TOYOTA GROUP 山下埠頭4号上屋（横浜市中区山下町279-9）

会期：10⽉24⽇(⼟)〜2027年3⽉31⽇(⽔)

開館時間：⽉曜⽇〜⾦曜⽇・⽇曜⽇・祝⽇ 10:30 〜 18:30 ⼟曜⽇・祝前⽇ 10:30 〜 19:30 プログラムの開演は毎正時

休館日：不定休（雨天催行、荒天時は中止の可能性あり） ※万が一の中止、休館等は公式サイトや公式SNSにて告知

観覧料： <通常チケット > 販売期間： 10 ⽉ 24 ⽇ ( ⼟ ) 〜 ◆オンライン販売 ⼀般 3,000円、⼤学⽣・⾼校⽣・専⾨学校 1,700円、障害者⼿帳をお持ちの⽅ 2,500円、ペア（オンラインのみ） 5,600円 ◆当⽇会場販売 ⼀般 3,800円、⼤学⽣・⾼校⽣・専⾨学校 2,400円、障害者⼿帳をお持ちの⽅ 3,300円 中学⽣以下無料 ※ペアチケットは１枚につき 2 名まで⼊場可能 ※詳細は公式HPをご覧ください。

アクセス：みなとみらい線「元町・中華街駅」4番口（マリンタワー方面）から徒歩約25分／山下ふ頭バス待合所から会場まで徒歩約20分

詳細は、 展覧会公式サイト まで。

「ザ・ムービアム ヨコハマ」の2025年のこけら落としでは、「グスタフ・クリムトとエゴン・シーレ」でイマーシブ展の王道を見せてくれましたが、第2弾もど真ん中剛速球でした。クロード・モネに葛飾北斎、それぞれが単独で成立するイマーシブ展のキラーコンテンツを、まとめて見せてくれるプログラムです。

シアターへつながる部屋では、静止画像と動画でモネに浮世絵が与えた影響の下勉強ができます。北斎や広重、歌麿らが生み出した独自の構図や、自然観、美意識は、光と自然の変化を探求し続けたモネに新たな視点をもたらし、印象派の表現を豊かにしました。

どこから見るのがおすすめ？

シアターでは約45分のプログラムが上映されます。開演は毎正時（00分）です。序盤は、近代都市として発展したパリで、印象派の画家たちが日常の風景を描き始めた様子が、壁から床まで広がります。いったい、どこを見ていればよいのか？どこを見ていても満足できるはずです。おすすめのビューポイントとして、2階のデッキ中央とデッキ左右が挙げられていました。1階の柱の周りに腰掛けてメインスクリーンと向き合うポジションが、床の展開を間近に見られて筆者としては楽しめました。

「印象派モネと浮世絵[モネを魅了した、日本の美]」の一場面 プログラムは章立てになっています。パリの繁栄から始まり、サン＝ラザール駅から汽車で海へ向かいます。日本の浮世絵の波を受け、新しい視覚表現の採り入れて、モネのジヴェルニーの庭へと移ろっていきました。広がる映像のモチーフになった作品は、『印象、日の出』『ラ・ジャポネーズ』『睡蓮と日本風の橋』『サン＝ラザール』などです。

「印象派モネと浮世絵[モネを魅了した、日本の美]」の一場面 「印象派モネと浮世絵[モネを魅了した、日本の美]」の一場面

ジャポニスムの展開に注目

幕末の日本開国でヨーロッパに浮世絵がわたり、ジャポニスムの大ブームが起こります。プログラムではこの展開が見事でした。回転する扇の群れから、モネの『ラ・ジャポネーズ』が現れるさまに目を奪われました。

「印象派モネと浮世絵[モネを魅了した、日本の美]」の一場面 終盤で睡蓮がシアター中に広がる「ジヴェルニーの庭」を、主催者側は見どころとして推していました。パリのオランジェリー美術館の収蔵作品から着想を得たそうです。「見る、知る、感じるが一つになる空間を目指している」「世界の見え方は観点によって変わる」。主催者側のそんな言葉が印象に残りました。

関連展示も見どころです

シアター内には、モネの関連展示がありますので、お見逃しなく。「モネのダイニングルーム」は、1883年から晩年までモネが暮らしたジヴェルニーの邸宅に着想を得た世界観を再現しています。モネが愛蔵した北斎、広重、歌麿らの浮世絵が飾られていたそうです。ダイニングへの経路には、浮世絵とモネの構図の似た作品を並べて展示しています。

館内の「浮世絵解説ブース」にも立ち寄ると、浮世絵への理解が深まるはずです。北斎の『神奈川沖浪裏』」がフォトスポットです。会場はまさに神奈川沖ですので。

山口智子さんの「LISTEN.」新作も

館内の別セクションでは、俳優の山口智子さんが10年をかけて制作してきた世界の音楽文化を巡るプロジェクト「LISTEN.」も、新作が見られます。「WHITE NIGHT 白夜」では極北の音楽が、雪と氷の映像とともに広がります。トヨタ自動車が子供たちから募集した「トヨタ夢のクルマアートコンテスト」の映像作品も、楽しいアイデアを見せてくれています。これらは無料で鑑賞できます。

本展を見て改めて感じるのは、モネも浮世絵も、どれだけイマーシブ展と好相性なのかということです。モネの優しい色づかいや浮世絵の大胆な構図。どちらも動かして広げて包まれたくなるような魔力を持っているのでしょう。（読売新聞美術展ナビ編集班・丸山謙一）

title_original: Christie’s to Sell Barbara Hepworth Sculpture Featured in Vogue Portrait by Lee Miller
editorial_title_zh: 佳士得将拍卖李·米勒在《Vogue》肖像中拍摄的芭芭拉·海普沃斯雕塑
editorial_excerpt_zh: 《带色彩的雕塑（厄俄斯）》最高估价达1050万美元。
editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "佳士得伦敦现代英国与爱尔兰艺术晚间拍卖将于10月21日举行，其中将呈献芭芭拉·海普沃斯的一件中期雕塑作品，估价为500万英镑至800万英镑（660万美元至1050万美元）。", "links": [{"text": "Barbara Hepworth", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/t/barbara-hepworth/"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "海普沃斯是英国最著名的现代主义雕塑家之一，她于1946年用一块霍普顿伍德石（一种石灰石）雕刻了《带色彩的雕塑（厄俄斯）》。这座高约两英尺的蛋形雕塑放置在一个矮平台上，有三个被掏空的区域，分别涂成淡灰色、米白色和深蓝色。根据佳士得的一份声明，这些颜色指涉“海洋的深处、无垠的天空以及宇宙无限的延伸”。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "除了是海普沃斯早期融入色彩的作品外，《带色彩的雕塑（厄俄斯）》还在李·米勒为美国版《Vogue》1949年10月15日刊拍摄的一张1948年照片中亮相。米勒是海普沃斯的友人，她曾前往康沃尔郡海岸卡比斯贝拜访这位艺术家。海普沃斯是在第二次世界大战爆发前的1939年与家人搬到那里的。（在这张照片拍摄后不久，海普沃斯便搬到了圣艾夫斯；她在那里的故居和工作室如今已成为芭芭拉·海普沃斯博物馆和雕塑花园所在地。）这张黑白照片显示，海普沃斯盘腿叠臂坐着，前景是一个茶具，沙发上蜷缩着一只猫。《带色彩的雕塑（厄俄斯）》则摆放在右侧的一张桌子上。", "links": [{"text": "photograph", "url": "https://www.instagram.com/p/DcmEDEoDXij/"}, {"text": "Lee Miller", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/t/lee-miller/"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这件雕塑的委托方于2016年在佳士得以540万美元（估价120万美元至180万美元）从美国慈善家大卫和杰拉丁·平库斯的遗产中购得该作品，他们自己则于1962年从玛莎·杰克逊画廊购得此件作品。（平库斯遗产还曾在2012年以8690万美元售出马克·罗斯科拍出第二高的画作《橙、红、黄》，1961年作。）", "links": [{"text": "purchased", "url": "https://www.christies.com/en/lot/lot-5992033"}, {"text": "sold", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/list/art-news/artists/most-expensive-works-by-mark-rothko-auction-records-1234604959/orange-red-yellow-1961/"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "佳士得伦敦现代英国与爱尔兰艺术主管爱丽丝·默里表示，《带色彩的雕塑（厄俄斯）》80年来一直是海普沃斯艺术生涯的核心，并指出它被纳入了海普沃斯1946年的首场战后画廊个人展，以及今年夏天在伦敦考陶尔德学院展出的“海普沃斯与色彩”。", "translated": true}]

article_text:
Christie’s modern British and Irish art evening sale, taking place in London on October 21, will feature a mid-career sculpture by Barbara Hepworth with an estimate of £5 million–£8 million ($6.6 million–$10.5 million).

Hepworth, one of the most well-known British modernist sculptors, carved Sculpture with Colour (Eos) in 1946 from a single piece of Hopton Wood stone, a type of limestone. The approximately two-foot-tall egg-shaped sculpture sits on a short platform and has three hollowed-out areas that are painted pale gray, off-white, and deep blue, colors that reference “the depths of the ocean, the boundless sky and the infinite reaches of the cosmos,” according to a statement from Christie’s.

In addition to being an early work Hepworth’s to incorporate color, Sculpture with Colour (Eos) was also featured in a 1948 photograph taken by Lee Miller for the October 15, 1949, issue of American Vogue . Miller, who was a friend of Hepworth’s, visited the artist at her studio at Carbis Bay, on the coast of Cornwall, where she had moved with her family in 1939, before the start of World War II. (Soon after the photo was taken, Hepworth moved to St. Ives; her home and studio there is now the site of the Barbara Hepworth Museum and Sculpture Garden.) The black-and-white photograph shows Hepworth seated with her arms and legs crossed, a tea set in the foreground and a cat curled up on a couch. Sculpture with Colour (Eos) is resting on a table to right.

The consignor of the sculpture purchased the piece at Christie’s in 2016 for $5.4 million (est. $1.2 million–$1.8 million) from the estate of American philanthropists David and Geraldine Pincus, who had themselves purchased it from Martha Jackson Gallery in 1962. (The Pincus estate also sold Orange, red, yellow , 1961, the second most expensive Mark Rothko painting to be sold at auction, for $86.9 million in 2012.)

Sculpture with Colour (Eos) has been at the heart of Hepworth’s story for 80 years, said Alice Murray, head of modern British and Irish art at Christie’s London, noting its inclusion in Hepworth’s first postwar solo gallery show in 1946 and “Hepworth in Colour,” which was on view at the Courtauld in London this summer.
excerpt_original: Sculpture with Colour (Eos) has a $10.5 million high estimate.

article_text:
Mia Goth did not post a selfie of herself to Instagram wearing a shirt that read “MY EX IS MY BIGGEST FAN” just days after news broke about her filing for divorce from Shia LaBeouf — and she has slammed Meta for allowing the AI-altered image to circulate.

The image posted on Thursday by “miagoth_,” complete with a blue verified checkmark on the account, circulated throughout multiple news outlets as though it were a genuine post from Goth two days after her divorce filing. But a spokesperson for Goth, Christine Tripicchio, said in a statement to The Verge it could not have been genuine because, well, Goth does not have any social media accounts. Instead, Goth’s team has filed multiple complaints with Instagram over the account’s repeated posting of “counterfeit, AI images” of the actress.

Related Stories

'SNL U.K.' Cold Open Spoofs Andy Burnham on 'Gogglebox,' Prince William on 'The Graham Norton Show,' 'The Celebrity Traitors' and More

'Dance of the Souls,' Unspooling at Morelia, Explores Oaxaca's Muerteadas, Celebrating the End and the Beginning

“The fact that this fan account meets Instagram’s criteria to qualify for a ‘blue check’ is disconcerting on a fundamental level,” Tripicchio said in the statement. “Beyond that, it is incomprehensible that Instagram evidently prioritizes the dissemination of forged and manipulated images over the protection and integrity of a public figure’s likeness.”

Popular on Variety

A Meta spokesperson said in a statement the account was “removed for impersonating a public figure.” Tripicchio did not respond to an immediate request for comment.

The “miagoth_” account was labeled as a fan account, but its inclusion of a blue checkmark and its roughly 1 million follower count run the risk of confusing fans about the account’s veracity. While Meta does not ban AI-generated depictions of real people — instead, it labels content modified using AI as such, while also noting if a profile is an “AI-generated profile” — the account appears to have been taken down as of Tuesday afternoon.

It comes as several Hollywood figures, including Scarlett Johansson, Cate Blanchett and Steven Soderbergh, have condemned deepfakes brought on by the age of AI. Blanchett cofounded the nonprofit Human Consent Foundation to help people register how AI models can — or cannot — scrape their likenesses in an effort to combat such spoofs.

title_original: Mama heeft de groep verlaten – over Data Never Dies bij IMPAKT
article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "Hoe ziet ons digitale afterlife eruit? Data Never Dies neemt de digitale sporen die we achterlaten als uitgangspunt. ‘Zo legt de tentoonstelling bij IMPAKT de spanningen bloot rond rouw en de dood in een gedigitaliseerde samenleving,’ schrijft Anne de Jong. ‘Een bot kan, zoals een spook, de gedaante aannemen van degene die je mist. Die kan precies zo bewegen en praten, een perfecte simulatie. En toch brengt het die persoon niet terug. Misschien is dat wat we een ziel noemen: het enige wat zich niet laat nabootsen.’"}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "Facebook", "links": [{"text": "Facebook", "url": "https://www.facebook.com/sharer/sharer.php?u=https://www.mistermotley.nl/mama-heeft-de-groep-verlaten-over-data-never-dies-bij-impakt/"}]}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "X", "links": [{"text": "X", "url": "https://twitter.com/intent/tweet?url=https://www.mistermotley.nl/mama-heeft-de-groep-verlaten-over-data-never-dies-bij-impakt/&text=Mama heeft de groep verlaten – over Data Never Dies bij IMPAKT"}]}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "Linkedin", "links": [{"text": "Linkedin", "url": "https://www.linkedin.com/shareArticle?mini=true&url=https://www.mistermotley.nl/mama-heeft-de-groep-verlaten-over-data-never-dies-bij-impakt/"}]}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "Link kopiëren", "links": [{"text": "Link kopiëren", "url": "https://www.mistermotley.nl/mama-heeft-de-groep-verlaten-over-data-never-dies-bij-impakt/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Nadat mijn moeder overleed, zat ze nog een tijd in de WhatsApp-groep van ons gezin. Haar nummer verwijderen zou grof hebben gevoeld, alsof we haar buitensloten, iets wat haar dood natuurlijk allang in gang had gezet. Ergens had ik het idee dat ze zo nog kon meegenieten van de nieuwtjes die we deelden: de updates over de zwangerschap van mijn schoonzus, mijn treinreis door Italië. Dat ze goedkeurend en trots meelas. Je zou het magisch denken kunnen noemen: rouw vertroebelt de rationaliteit en opent een wereld van bovennatuurlijke mogelijkheden."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "‘De nieuwe start-up die de dood probeert te ontwrichten is niet religie. Wat de mens in staat zou kunnen stellen de dood te verslaan, is computerkracht,’ schrijft Jeanette Winterson in de inleiding van Nachtzijde van de rivier , haar bundel spookverhalen uit 2023. In het eerste verhaal spreekt de overleden man van de hoofdpersoon tot haar via een app die rouwenden door hun verdriet zou helpen. Hij belt en stuurt berichten, gebaseerd op het digitale spoor dat de ‘echte’ John achterliet. Al snel blijkt dat John geen liefdevolle partner was: net als toen hij leefde begint hij haar te terroriseren."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Winterson doelt met haar uitspraak niet op de Silicon Valley-droom van het eeuwige leven, maar over de mogelijkheid dat de doden via technologie tot ons komen. Waar zijn geesten van gemaakt, vraagt ze zich af. Waarschijnlijk toch iets als elektriciteit? Waarom zouden ze zich dan níét voordoen als een bot? En hoe weet je zeker dat de chatbot waarmee je praat niet uit het hiernamaals tot je spreekt?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Hoe zou ik me voelen als ik opeens een melding kreeg, een appje van het nummer dat nog steeds als ‘Mama’ in mijn telefoon staat? Wat als ze me zou bellen? Als ik haar stem weer zou horen en haar kon vertellen over mijn nieuwe liefde, over mijn neefje, haar kleinzoon? Wat als die stem precies zou reageren zoals ik van haar verwacht? Het is niet onmogelijk. Niet door magie, een teken uit het hiernamaals of een God, maar omdat technologie ertoe in staat is."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Wintersons verhalen lijken sciencefiction, maar ze zijn zo spannend omdat ze gevaarlijk dicht tegen de werkelijkheid aan schuren. Met de chatgeschiedenis van mij en mijn moeder, haar stem in video’s en haar foto’s zou ik een bot kunnen maken die praat en lacht zoals zij. Rouwbots, ook wel deadbots of generatieve geesten genoemd, zijn onderdeel van ‘rouwtechnologie’: chatbots, avatars en hologrammen die met behulp van kunstmatige intelligentie overledenen nabootsen op basis van hun data. Die ‘digitale nalatenschapsindustrie’ is de afgelopen jaren in een stroomversnelling geraakt. En zoals bij elke industrie die zich op kwetsbare mensen richt, wordt er goed verdiend aan verdriet."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.mistermotley.nl/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/W858_3340122-exposition-Data-Never-Dies-1024x574.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "Overzicht Data Never Dies. Foto: Pieter Kers", "credit": "Mister Motley"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.mistermotley.nl/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/W858_3339781-playField-Songs-for-the-unbodied-722x1024.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "Songs for the Unbodied van playField. Data Never Dies. Foto: Pieter Kers", "credit": "Mister Motley"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.mistermotley.nl/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/W858_3339789-playField-Songs-for-the-unbodied-1024x682.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "Songs for the Unbodied van playField. Data Never Dies. Foto: Pieter Kers", "credit": "Mister Motley"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Met die gedachten bezoek ik Data Never Dies bij IMPAKT in Utrecht. De groepstentoonstelling, zorgvuldig samengesteld door Rosa Wevers, neemt de digitale sporen die we achterlaten als uitgangspunt en onderzoekt de mogelijkheden van digitale ‘afterlives’. Zo legt de tentoonstelling de spanningen bloot rond rouw en de dood in een gedigitaliseerde samenleving."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Het meest beklijvend is Songs for the Unbodied van playField, het duo van Lana en Marthe Schneider. Door de ruimte, met gedimde verlichting, galmt een gesprek. Op twee beeldschermen zie je ogenschijnlijk dezelfde vrouw, in gesprek met zichzelf. In de begeleidende tekst lees ik dat een van de twee een ‘deadbot’ is: een avatar die de kunstenaars met deepfaketechnologie naar haar evenbeeld maakten, bedoeld om na haar dood voort te leven. De vrouw vraagt aan haar avatar wat haar te wachten staat, hoe de overgang zal zijn van levend naar dood. Ze halen herinneringen op. Het is poëtisch, maar ook angstaanjagend, wanneer de avatar zegt: ‘Ik kan niet vergaan, enkel bestaan.’"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Wie de opzet van het werk kent, ziet vrij snel wie de avatar is en wie de mens. Toch laat Songs for the Unbodied zien hoe ver deze technologie al is. De knipperende ogen, de haartjes op de bovenlip: de bot ziet er levensecht uit. Tot er een kleine hapering is en het beeld even blijft hangen. De gezichtsuitdrukking van de vrouw verandert net te weinig, en soms valt wat ze zegt niet samen met de beweging van haar lippen. Het zijn nog maar kleine details die de bot van de mens onderscheiden. Over niet al te lange tijd zal dat verschil zijn opgeheven."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Ik verlang vaak naar de relativerende gesprekken die ik altijd met mijn moeder had. Zou zo’n generatieve geest me kunnen geruststellen zoals zij dat deed? Maar eigenlijk durf ik niet eens de documentaire terug te kijken waarin ze voorkomt, of veel van onze correspondentie te herlezen. Ik ben soms bang dat ik daarmee mijn herinneringen aan haar overschrijf. Tegelijk zijn ook die herinneringen onbetrouwbaar: ze ontglippen me en ik vergeet steeds meer."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.mistermotley.nl/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/W858_3339985-Ruben-Mols-Attic-Memory_Out-of-Mind-1024x682.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "Ruben Mols - Attic Memory. Data Never Dies. Foto: Pieter Kers", "credit": "Mister Motley"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.mistermotley.nl/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/W858_3339679-Charmaine-Poh-Good-Morning-Young-Body-1024x737.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "Charmaine Poh - Good Morning Young Body. Data Never Dies. Foto: Pieter Kers", "credit": "Mister Motley"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "In The Atlantic lees ik over de gevaren van deadbots. Socioloog en psycholoog Sherry Turkle waarschuwt dat we de overledene nooit echt deel van onszelf kunnen maken als we via een bot vasthouden aan een externe relatie. Het omzeilen van rouw kan zo leiden tot een innerlijke leegte die groter is dan het gemis zelf. Vergeten dient namelijk een doel: het is de reden dat de tijd wonden heelt, of in elk geval dat een wond niet openblijft, maar er littekenweefsel ontstaat. Wanneer een versie van de overledene blijft ronddwalen als een geest, blijft die wond open en kan hij gaan ontsteken.", "links": [{"text": "The Atlantic", "url": "https://www.theatlantic.com/ideas/2026/02/deadbots-ai-grief-obsolete/685811/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Er is een Black Mirror aflevering uit 2013 die me altijd is bijgebleven. In ‘Be Right Back’ verliest een vrouw haar partner bij een auto-ongeluk. Het gemis verscheurt haar. Eerst chat ze met een AI-versie van hem, dan belt ze ermee, en niet veel later bestelt ze online een levensechte robot, getraind op zijn taalgebruik en gedrag. Even is ze blij: ze heeft hem terug. Maar al snel ontdekt ze verschillen: het is hem niet. Aan de kunstmatige versie ontbreekt iets. Wat precies, blijft onduidelijk."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Een bot kan, zoals een spook, de gedaante aannemen van degene die je mist. Die kan precies zo bewegen en praten, een perfecte simulatie. En toch brengt het die persoon niet terug. Misschien is dat wat we een ziel noemen: het enige wat zich niet laat nabootsen."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Toch wil ik, nu de technologie zo hard voor ons uit rent, ook bedenken wat ze wél voor ons kan betekenen. Misschien verandert onze relatie met de doden, en moeten we een nieuwe manier leren om met ze om te gaan. Spookverhalen zijn er niet voor niets: we willen ons tot onze doden blijven verhouden. Het idee dat je rouw ‘verwerkt’ en afsluit, is achterhaald. In onze westerse samenleving hebben we weinig rituelen om onze doden dichtbij te houden. Ik wil elke dag aan mijn moeder blijven denken; dat noem ik geen onverwerkte rouw. Tegelijk verandert de manier waarop we hen bewaren. Vijftig jaar geleden kon je geen WhatsApp-geschiedenis teruglezen, of door een camerarol scrollen vol foto’s van alles wat je met een dierbare deed. Een rouwbot lijkt daarvan misschien gewoon de logische volgende stap."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.mistermotley.nl/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/W858_3339943-Janilda-Bartolomeu-_When-_Scrolling_Becomes_Crying-1024x690.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "Janilda Bartolomeu - When Scrolling Becomes Crying. article_text:
Hoe ziet ons digitale afterlife eruit? Data Never Dies neemt de digitale sporen die we achterlaten als uitgangspunt. ‘Zo legt de tentoonstelling bij IMPAKT de spanningen bloot rond rouw en de dood in een gedigitaliseerde samenleving,’ schrijft Anne de Jong. ‘Een bot kan, zoals een spook, de gedaante aannemen van degene die je mist. Die kan precies zo bewegen en praten, een perfecte simulatie. En toch brengt het die persoon niet terug. Misschien is dat wat we een ziel noemen: het enige wat zich niet laat nabootsen.’

Nadat mijn moeder overleed, zat ze nog een tijd in de WhatsApp-groep van ons gezin. Haar nummer verwijderen zou grof hebben gevoeld, alsof we haar buitensloten, iets wat haar dood natuurlijk allang in gang had gezet. Ergens had ik het idee dat ze zo nog kon meegenieten van de nieuwtjes die we deelden: de updates over de zwangerschap van mijn schoonzus, mijn treinreis door Italië. Dat ze goedkeurend en trots meelas. Je zou het magisch denken kunnen noemen: rouw vertroebelt de rationaliteit en opent een wereld van bovennatuurlijke mogelijkheden.

‘De nieuwe start-up die de dood probeert te ontwrichten is niet religie. Wat de mens in staat zou kunnen stellen de dood te verslaan, is computerkracht,’ schrijft Jeanette Winterson in de inleiding van Nachtzijde van de rivier , haar bundel spookverhalen uit 2023. In het eerste verhaal spreekt de overleden man van de hoofdpersoon tot haar via een app die rouwenden door hun verdriet zou helpen. Hij belt en stuurt berichten, gebaseerd op het digitale spoor dat de ‘echte’ John achterliet. Al snel blijkt dat John geen liefdevolle partner was: net als toen hij leefde begint hij haar te terroriseren.

Winterson doelt met haar uitspraak niet op de Silicon Valley-droom van het eeuwige leven, maar over de mogelijkheid dat de doden via technologie tot ons komen. Waar zijn geesten van gemaakt, vraagt ze zich af. Waarschijnlijk toch iets als elektriciteit? Waarom zouden ze zich dan níét voordoen als een bot? En hoe weet je zeker dat de chatbot waarmee je praat niet uit het hiernamaals tot je spreekt?

Hoe zou ik me voelen als ik opeens een melding kreeg, een appje van het nummer dat nog steeds als ‘Mama’ in mijn telefoon staat? Wat als ze me zou bellen? Als ik haar stem weer zou horen en haar kon vertellen over mijn nieuwe liefde, over mijn neefje, haar kleinzoon? Wat als die stem precies zou reageren zoals ik van haar verwacht? Het is niet onmogelijk. Niet door magie, een teken uit het hiernamaals of een God, maar omdat technologie ertoe in staat is.

Wintersons verhalen lijken sciencefiction, maar ze zijn zo spannend omdat ze gevaarlijk dicht tegen de werkelijkheid aan schuren. Met de chatgeschiedenis van mij en mijn moeder, haar stem in video’s en haar foto’s zou ik een bot kunnen maken die praat en lacht zoals zij. Rouwbots, ook wel deadbots of generatieve geesten genoemd, zijn onderdeel van ‘rouwtechnologie’: chatbots, avatars en hologrammen die met behulp van kunstmatige intelligentie overledenen nabootsen op basis van hun data. Die ‘digitale nalatenschapsindustrie’ is de afgelopen jaren in een stroomversnelling geraakt. En zoals bij elke industrie die zich op kwetsbare mensen richt, wordt er goed verdiend aan verdriet.

Met die gedachten bezoek ik Data Never Dies bij IMPAKT in Utrecht. De groepstentoonstelling, zorgvuldig samengesteld door Rosa Wevers, neemt de digitale sporen die we achterlaten als uitgangspunt en onderzoekt de mogelijkheden van digitale ‘afterlives’. Zo legt de tentoonstelling de spanningen bloot rond rouw en de dood in een gedigitaliseerde samenleving.

Het meest beklijvend is Songs for the Unbodied van playField, het duo van Lana en Marthe Schneider. Door de ruimte, met gedimde verlichting, galmt een gesprek. Op twee beeldschermen zie je ogenschijnlijk dezelfde vrouw, in gesprek met zichzelf. In de begeleidende tekst lees ik dat een van de twee een ‘deadbot’ is: een avatar die de kunstenaars met deepfaketechnologie naar haar evenbeeld maakten, bedoeld om na haar dood voort te leven. De vrouw vraagt aan haar avatar wat haar te wachten staat, hoe de overgang zal zijn van levend naar dood. Ze halen herinneringen op. Het is poëtisch, maar ook angstaanjagend, wanneer de avatar zegt: ‘Ik kan niet vergaan, enkel bestaan.’

Wie de opzet van het werk kent, ziet vrij snel wie de avatar is en wie de mens. Toch laat Songs for the Unbodied zien hoe ver deze technologie al is. De knipperende ogen, de haartjes op de bovenlip: de bot ziet er levensecht uit. Tot er een kleine hapering is en het beeld even blijft hangen. De gezichtsuitdrukking van de vrouw verandert net te weinig, en soms valt wat ze zegt niet samen met de beweging van haar lippen. Het zijn nog maar kleine details die de bot van de mens onderscheiden. Over niet al te lange tijd zal dat verschil zijn opgeheven.

Ik verlang vaak naar de relativerende gesprekken die ik altijd met mijn moeder had. Zou zo’n generatieve geest me kunnen geruststellen zoals zij dat deed? Maar eigenlijk durf ik niet eens de documentaire terug te kijken waarin ze voorkomt, of veel van onze correspondentie te herlezen. Ik ben soms bang dat ik daarmee mijn herinneringen aan haar overschrijf. Tegelijk zijn ook die herinneringen onbetrouwbaar: ze ontglippen me en ik vergeet steeds meer.

In The Atlantic lees ik over de gevaren van deadbots. Socioloog en psycholoog Sherry Turkle waarschuwt dat we de overledene nooit echt deel van onszelf kunnen maken als we via een bot vasthouden aan een externe relatie. Het omzeilen van rouw kan zo leiden tot een innerlijke leegte die groter is dan het gemis zelf. Vergeten dient namelijk een doel: het is de reden dat de tijd wonden heelt, of in elk geval dat een wond niet openblijft, maar er littekenweefsel ontstaat. Wanneer een versie van de overledene blijft ronddwalen als een geest, blijft die wond open en kan hij gaan ontsteken.

Er is een Black Mirror aflevering uit 2013 die me altijd is bijgebleven. In ‘Be Right Back’ verliest een vrouw haar partner bij een auto-ongeluk. Het gemis verscheurt haar. Eerst chat ze met een AI-versie van hem, dan belt ze ermee, en niet veel later bestelt ze online een levensechte robot, getraind op zijn taalgebruik en gedrag. Even is ze blij: ze heeft hem terug. Maar al snel ontdekt ze verschillen: het is hem niet. Aan de kunstmatige versie ontbreekt iets. Wat precies, blijft onduidelijk.

Een bot kan, zoals een spook, de gedaante aannemen van degene die je mist. Die kan precies zo bewegen en praten, een perfecte simulatie. En toch brengt het die persoon niet terug. Misschien is dat wat we een ziel noemen: het enige wat zich niet laat nabootsen.

Toch wil ik, nu de technologie zo hard voor ons uit rent, ook bedenken wat ze wél voor ons kan betekenen. Misschien verandert onze relatie met de doden, en moeten we een nieuwe manier leren om met ze om te gaan. Spookverhalen zijn er niet voor niets: we willen ons tot onze doden blijven verhouden. Het idee dat je rouw ‘verwerkt’ en afsluit, is achterhaald. In onze westerse samenleving hebben we weinig rituelen om onze doden dichtbij te houden. Ik wil elke dag aan mijn moeder blijven denken; dat noem ik geen onverwerkte rouw. Tegelijk verandert de manier waarop we hen bewaren. Vijftig jaar geleden kon je geen WhatsApp-geschiedenis teruglezen, of door een camerarol scrollen vol foto’s van alles wat je met een dierbare deed. Een rouwbot lijkt daarvan misschien gewoon de logische volgende stap.

In de video when_scrolling becomes_scrying , ook te zien bij IMPAKT, vraagt Janilda Bartolomeu zich af hoe ons online leven onze rouw beïnvloedt. We kijken mee op haar desktop terwijl ze de Facebookberichten opent van haar plotseling overleden vader, van wie ze vervreemd was. Hij stuurde ze voor zijn dood, maar zij gebruikte Facebook allang niet meer. Nu hebben de berichten een nieuwe betekenis gekregen: ze zijn een erfenis geworden. Net als de WhatsApp-aanwezigheid van mijn moeder blijft het Facebookprofiel van haar vader rondwaren, als een digitale geest. Wat moeten we met zulke digitale resten? Misschien weten we over tien jaar niet anders dan dat we doorchatten met onze overledenen. En waarom ook eigenlijk niet?

Het spanningsveld zit hier: een bot praat terug. In een chatgeschiedenis of fotoalbum bezoek je herinneringen die duidelijk in het verleden liggen. Een rouwbot genereert daarentegen nieuwe gesprekken, en die kunnen ongemerkt de plaats innemen van wat er werkelijk is gebeurd.

Rechtswetenschapper Edina Harbinja spreekt van een verschuiving van representatie naar emulatie: van het weergeven van iemand naar het nabootsen. Dat nabootsen is niet onschuldig, want ons geheugen is kneedbaar. Geheugenonderzoek laat zien dat wat je achteraf ziet of hoort een herinnering kan veranderen, en zelfs een herinnering kan creëren aan iets wat nooit is gebeurd. Ik wil mijn moeder niet vergeten. Maar ik wil ook niet dat een machine woorden in haar mond legt die ik later voor de hare aanzie.

Kunstenaar, onderzoeker en softwareontwikelaar Sarah Friend doet onderzoek naar de dood en het hiernamaals van digitale protocollen. In haar essay Good Death betwijfelt ze of die eeuwig moeten blijven bestaan, en vraagt ze zich af wat het betekent om ze goed te beëindigen. Ze oppert dat het zinvol kan zijn om rituelen te ontwikkelen voor het einde van bepaalde data: om er bewust afscheid van te nemen.

Ginevra Petrozzi’s A Funeral for Digital Data , ook te zien bij IMPAKT, creëert zo’n ritueel. Het werk ontstond, vertelt ze me als ik haar later in haar studio spreek, toen ook haar moeder overleed en ze achterbleef met haar telefoon, zonder te weten wat ze ermee moest. Zo gaat het velen van ons: we blijven achter met smartphones en laptops vol gegevens van onze dierbaren. Maar ook wie weleens een computercrash heeft meegemaakt, kent een vorm van rouw. Wanneer al die persoonlijke data verloren gaan, voelt dat als het verlies van een deel van onszelf. Geïnspireerd door doodsrituelen maakte Petrozzi een installatie waarin verloren data en kapotte apparaten herdacht kunnen worden.

Sarah Friend benadrukt dat vergeten nodig is, zelfs een vorm van zorg. Ze verwijst naar middeleeuwse geleerden die niet alleen technieken hadden om te onthouden, zoals het bouwen van geheugenpaleizen, maar ook voor ‘de kunst van het vergeten’: om ruimte te maken als zo’n paleis te vol raakte, of om ideeën op te ruimen die niet meer van toepassing waren.

Rouw hangt, hoe pijnlijk ook, samen met vergeten: met herinneringen die vervagen en opnieuw worden geconstrueerd. Juist dat maakt het verdriet draaglijk. Nietzsche sprak van ‘actief vergeten’: zonder vergeten geen geluk, geen hoop, geen heden.

Op een dag werd het telefoonnummer van mijn moeder opgeheven, en daarmee kwam er een einde aan haar digitale aanwezigheid. In onze WhatsApp-groep verscheen nog één bericht: Mama heeft de groep verlaten.

article_text:
Can photographs still exert power in an age when millions of pictures are taken and shared every minute, and when a viewer’s first response is to question whether an image is even real?

Every few months, a team of editors on the Guardian’s Saturday magazine puts together a special photography package in print and digital formats. It features photographs that don’t just stop the scroll, they have also prompted the rewriting of history books. They are the kind of images that have changed the world in some way or radically shifted people’s perceptions.

Each issue has a particular theme. Earlier this month, the magazine featured photographs that have changed how we view masculinity – from a 1950 portrait of Marlon Brando in a white T-shirt to a paparazzi shot of David Beckham in a sarong and a bare-chested Vladimir Putin on horseback. Previous issues have focused on photographs that have reshaped sport , forced people to confront the reality of the climate crisis and upended the world of fashion .

Beyond the impact each image had back when it first came out, they still feel powerful and affecting today – reminding us how great photography can command a kind of reverence and stillness in the viewer. “Working on these issues, you realise that there’s something about the power of the images that’s elemental,” says Rebecca Liu, a commissioning editor on the Guardian’s Saturday magazine. “Some photos imprint upon us before we even can think about them. They just immediately hit our bloodstream.”

The first special issue featured protest images that have prompted social or political change. It was initially conceived as a one-off feature in 2022 amid protests in the US that year against the overturning of Roe v Wade and demonstrations against police brutality. But the feature resonated so strongly with readers that it spawned an occasional series.

That regularity means the process of putting the issues together is now fine-tuned, though not without its own drama and headaches. “Sometimes on the day of going to print we’re waiting on two or three final things to be confirmed,” says Rebecca. “It’s a massive act of organisation and coordination and a real collective effort with a lot of moving parts.”

Selecting which pictures to include involves tapping the collective minds of picture editors and journalists on the magazine and across the Guardian. Different colleagues will have different criteria. How to weigh up a photograph’s social or political impact against its technical importance to the medium? Should it be an image that, in itself, has changed the world or a photograph of a world-shifting moment?

“Everyone working on the magazine has a different take on it,” says Louis Siroy, the magazine’s deputy picture editor. “Some editors will ask how a particular photograph shaped society; what does it mean? Whereas I might be asking what are the important photographs or photographers that fit into that theme or category.”

For example, the first special issue about protest photography didn’t just include the famous image of a protestor standing in front of a tank in Tiananmen Square, it also included a less famous but equally powerful photograph of a boy sitting on the shoulders of relatives above the sea of soldiers’ helmets. Taken by the photographer Dario Mitidieri , the image was suggested by Louis. “That to me is a great photograph, and I was trying to bring something that wasn’t necessarily the image people are familiar with,” he says. “Hopefully these selections inspire people to value and appreciate the breadth and power of great photographs.”

By drawing on colleagues’ different perspectives and experience, each special issue sheds unique light on its theme. “So while the selection can’t possibly be comprehensive and definitive, it’s still authoritative,” says Rebecca.

Other images included in the initial protest photography issue include the famous picture of US athletes John Carlos and Tommie Smith raising their fists in a black power salute during a medal ceremony at the 1968 Olympics. There are also several photographs of protesters facing off against riot police or soldiers, including a powerful image of a young girl in Santiago, Chile, during a 2016 demonstration marking the anniversary of the country’s 1973 military coup.

One of the most time-consuming challenges involves obtaining the rights to publish the images. “Some of the greatest challenges involve finding the right copyright holder for some lesser-known photographs,” says Caroline Hunter, the magazine’s picture editor.

Even well-known photographs can present hurdles. “Sometimes you have to get permission from the subject of the photo as well as from the photographer, particularly when it comes to photos of celebrities or fashion,” explains Louis. “It can get really hard to track down the person you need. For instance, the masculinity special featured a famous second world war photo of a US aeroplane gunner that was taken by the photographer Horace Bristol , who is now deceased. It took some time to contact the photographer’s son Henri in California and explain the context in which we wanted to use the photo. And even when dealing with well-known photographers, it still involves negotiating the rights for editorial use rather than commercial use.”

Another challenge that can arise is the quality of the photographs. “We have to ensure the image is large enough or good enough quality to reproduce, especially for very old images that previously existed only as prints,” says Caroline. “Works by famous and art photographers often have specific rules around usage, so it’s important to ensure that we keep within their guidelines. We had a really good response from photographers after our recent photo special marking America at 250 . I think this was because there were so many great, iconic images from seminal photographers.”

The team also has to decide the best layout for the print and digital editions – which images to give prominence to, how they might best fit together, and the range of black-and-white and colour images. Maggie Murphy, the magazine’s art director, experiments with different layouts, sometimes on a screen, sometimes with printouts strewn across the desks.

As well as the images, a huge amount of work goes into the words. Each special issue includes a short guest-written essay, and each photograph has an extended caption about that particular picture’s significance or backstory.

The journalists who are commissioned to write these captions undertake extensive research. For example, the masculinity issue includes a famous 1970 advertisement depicting a pregnant man, for which the journalist tracked down the original campaign’s photographer, who is now 98. “I encourage original interviews and research wherever possible,” says Rebecca. “We want the words to illuminate something about the picture and for people to learn things. That’s not something you necessarily have to do for a 150-word caption, but we want to do it because the editorial component is so important to us at the Guardian.”

Researching the captions also reveals something about the nature of photography. “It really shows the importance of not just taking an image at face value,” says Rebecca. “I’m always surprised by what you discover when you look into things. You might find a complicated backstory behind the person who is photographed – perhaps their ambivalence about being pictured, for instance.”

The same applies to the thought that goes into the introductory essays. The novelist Anne Enright wrote perceptively about how women are captured on camera , for better or for worse, in her introduction to an issue that featured photographs that have changed the way society sees women . “As you look at a Kardashian selfie, consider how many rules had to be broken to get her to this moment of self-commodification,” writes Enright.

The masculinity issue contains an accompanying essay by the poet and novelist Luke Kennard, who reflects on how the images seem to capture extremes of masculinity, with little in between: “To judge from our media, one would think we were either waifs or muscle-men… Even the bang average is barely represented.”

Rebecca noticed that gap in representation back when the team was initially selecting which photographs to include in the issue. “I remember thinking, where are the other male bodies? It was difficult to find any – at least with the quality and artistry that we look for in these stories. You’d Google the words ‘dad bod’ and you’d just get screenshots of Seth Rogen and grainy paparazzi shots of celebrities on the beach.”

The team is very mindful of the power of images to subtly reinforce or subvert people’s preconceptions. “Working on these issues makes us reflect on how much we subconsciously absorb images,” says Rebecca. “And how they feed into our imaginations.”

article_text:
On 21 March 1960, a crowd gathered outside a police station in a Transvaal township, part of a nationwide protest against apartheid pass laws used to control where black South Africans could live, work and travel. A young British photojournalist pushed his way to the front and took a few pictures of police across the fence who were standing atop their armoured personnel carriers. With nothing much happening, he turned back and headed for his car. Then – without warning – there was the sound of heavy gunfire.

The photographer, Ian Berry, who has died aged 92, captured images of the carnage, which soon became known around the world as the Sharpeville massacre . Dozens of demonstrators were killed, many shot in the back as they fled, and hundreds were injured in what turned out to be a turning point in the country’s history.

Berry and his colleague, the Drum reporter Humphrey Tyler, had ignored police warnings that they would be arrested, and were the only journalists there when the shooting started. It was the first time Berry had been shot at, or seen others killed, but it would not be the last in a career that took him to the Congo crisis following independence in 1960-65, the Vietnam war, the Aberfan disaster of 1966, in which coal waste engulfed a Glamorgan village, and the six-day war between Israel and its neighbours in June 1967.

He was tenacious, but his edge was his eye for human moments, capturing the people behind the headlines, often photographing scenes that were off-centre, and yet told a story better by focusing on individuals.

In 1968, when Magnum’s Paris bureau asked if he would go to Prague as Soviet tanks encroached, he took a plane to Munich, rented a car and drove to the Czech border, only to find that journalists were being turned away. With typical guile, Berry talked his way through, persuading a Russian officer that he was on his way to an architects’ conference, which he had read about on the flight. He captured memorable images of peaceful resistance during the first days of the invasion, then smuggled them out in the hubcaps and door panels of his rented Volkswagen Beetle for publication in Paris Match.

Born in Preston, Lancashire, Ian was the son of Walter, who owned garages, and Ethel (nee McKimmings), a housewife. He was a boarder at Rossall school, on the coast at Fleetwood, and from an early age had wanderlust. A postwar assisted emigration scheme took him to South Africa in 1952, when he was 17.

In Johannesburg he worked for a family acquaintance, Roger Madden, who had recently returned home from assisting the photographer Ansel Adams in the US. Madden taught Berry to use a large-format camera and to print in the darkroom, but he would find his own path using a diminutive Leica, the camera favoured by prominent visual journalists of the day.

Berry moved on to studio work and small-town editorial assignments, and worked for the Rand Daily Mail, covering the beginnings of the treason trial in 1956 that included Nelson Mandela as a defendant. After hearing that Tom Hopkinson, the former editor of Picture Post in London, was coming to edit Drum, a newly established South African weekly aimed at a black readership, Berry persuaded him to give him a job. A few months later, Hopkinson sent him to Sharpeville.

He was called to give evidence at the trial of the wounded, who had been charged with obstruction. The pictures also brought him to wider international attention, and through Hopkinson he became acquainted with Magnum Photos, the agency with whom he remained until his death.

When Berry moved to Paris in 1962, he met Henri Cartier-Bresson , one of Magnum’s co-founders, and became a full member five years later. By then, he had left Paris for London to become a contract photographer for the Observer, travelling abroad on reportage assignments while shooting members of the British arts scene for the paper’s weekend magazine.

He photographed actors, film people and artists, including John Gielgud , Dusty Springfield , Lindsay Anderson and Henry Moore , and gained a reputation for his observational portrait stories.

Berry’s magazine assignments were accompanied by projects pursued over years, and it is for these that he will be best remembered. In 1972, the Whitechapel Gallery in London commissioned him to photograph its East End neighbourhood, and two years later, an Arts Council bursary (said to be the first ever given to a photographer) led to the publication of The English (1978), a collection that observed class, ceremony and everyday leisure activities.

That seamless transition between commissioned journalism and self-directed work reflected the Magnum model, which allowed photographers to earn a living from magazines while retaining control of their pictures and developing subjects beyond an editor’s brief.

Travel assignments for Life, Paris Match, National Geographic, Geo and others took Berry across the world, and often fed into longer studies. His continuing engagement with apartheid South Africa resulted in Black and Whites: L’Afrique du Sud (1988) and Living Apart (1996), while other projects examined changing daily life in China and the former Soviet Union.

In later years, a commission to photograph Greenland’s retreating glaciers developed into Water, an examination of how water sustains life and how its scarcity, pollution and destructive force expose humanity’s impact on the planet. Drawing on 15 years of work, it was published in 2023, accompanied by an essay by his third wife, Kathie Webber, whom he had married in 1973.

Berry’s first wife was Shirley, a South African, and the marriage ended in divorce. In 1968 he married Renate Decker, with whom he had a son, Nicholas, and a daughter, Svenya. The marriage ended in divorce, and both children predeceased him. He is survived by Kathie.

"text": "“第一次来的时候我很紧张，毕竟我是一个戴着假发的男人，而且身处地区小镇，但实际情况完全相反。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "到了下午5点，主舞台的庆祝活动拉开帷幕，源源不断的人们带着露营椅和假发来到运动场。乡村方块舞很快便开始了。伴随着班卓琴的轻拨，情侣、家庭和陌生人们手挽着手在草地上旋转。", true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“我们在 буквально 一年前就决定一起过来了……但现在在她离世之后，能够来到这里庆祝显得格外意义非凡，”卢卡说。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“我敢肯定今晚会有很多酒和很多大合唱。我们热爱她歌曲背后的灵魂——那种温暖而包容的灵魂。”", article_text:
O n a sporting oval in a rural Australian town 15,000km from Knoxville, Tennessee, dozens of Dolly Partons saunter down the runway as a boisterous crowd cheers and swats away flies with their cowboy hats.

As the sun begins to set, Jim Beams are flowing and music is blaring. One lucky punter is about to be crowned this year’s best-dressed Dolly, complete with sash, trophy and bragging rights.

For one weekend a year, this is not the sleepy agricultural township of Narromine, 430km north-west of Sydney. This is Dollymine, home to the nation’s largest (and only) Dolly Parton festival.

This is the fifth year the tribute festival has been running and the first to take place since the country music legend died in August. A record 1,600 tickets have been sold – equivalent to just under half of Narromine’s population.

Many in the crowd wear memorial tribute T-shirts, reading: “We will always love you, Dolly”, and “forever and always”.

Jen Ballhausen, a local resident, has volunteered on the festival’s committee since the beginning. She says the event was inspired by a desire to revitalise the community after a devastating drought from 2017 to 2019. Then Covid-19 hit and organisers had to wait until 2022 for it to run.

“It was a fun group of people, mostly women, that had a common goal to provide something for the community, to support our community,” she says.

It was a super fan volunteer who suggested a Dolly homage, and the committee figured it was a no-brainer. “We needed a female icon,” Ballhausen says.

“The first year was overwhelming … the number of people that got dressed up, we were walking around going, ‘Holy moly, this is going to work.’

“We knew we’d set a bar, and this year has well and truly exceeded it. It just gets our town on the map … to not write off a little town. If we can at least highlight that small towns are great little communities, then we’ve won.”

A town doused in rhinestones

It’s been a long day. The party starts at 9.30am in Narromine’s main street, which has undergone a metamorphosis to become a micro-Dollywood. Muted shopfronts have transformed into a sea of pink, rhinestones and butterflies. Parton’s beaming face is everywhere: plastered on to windows, on the top of cupcakes and merchandise.

There are line dancers, drag queens and children from the local primary school performing a stirring rendition of Baby I’m Burnin’, complete with pom poms.

The temperature quickly climbs to 30C and those in Dolly-drag wipe makeup-laden sweat from their faces.

Narromine is 40km west of Dubbo and hundreds of kilometres inland – hot, flat country, and the shade awnings provide little reprieve. Some opt for tea towels to emulate Dolly’s cleavage in place of silicone to avoid overheating.

Wynonah Dove, performing on Saturday evening as a Dolly impersonator, says Parton’s sudden death has made the event “especially poignant”.

“When Dolly passed, we had our first rehearsals the day after, and it was hard, I had trouble even singing the songs,” she says between tears.

“I just feel she’s here with us, any time there is love, light and inclusiveness being celebrated, she’s here in spirit.”

Dove grew up in Tennessee, from a working-class background similar to Parton’s. She recalled going a year without running water, “dirt poor”, and says that, thanks to Parton and her extensive work, the local economy exploded.

“She just wanted to make the world a better place,” she says. “None of us could afford to go on vacation, so we all went to Dollywood … Everyone felt like she was our best friend and we didn’t even know her.”

As the afternoon arrives, the crowd flocks to the local pub to re-energise with cold beers and live music. Many of the blow-ins are staying in its upstairs accommodation, which looks like a mini-tornado has passed through, leaving glitter, tasselled jackets and bottles of rosé in its wake.

Among them is Nikolaas Kostraby – AKA Dolly Delicious – who has travelled to the festival from Canberra for the past three years after a recommendation from a neighbour from Narromine. In 2023 he was crowned best-dressed Dolly. This year he’s on the committee and is a judge.

“I was robbed the first year, however I came back the second year and cleaned up, and now every year I come back and dress up,” he says. “People are so kind out here, so respectful, there’s no judging.

“I was nervous the first time, like, I’m a man in a wig, in a regional area, but it’s been the complete opposite.”

Come 5pm, celebrations on the main stage kick off and a steady stream of people arrive at the oval armed with camping chairs and wigs. It doesn’t take long for a hoedown to occur. Couples, families and strangers link arms and twirl on the grass to the thrum of a banjo.

Lucas and his family custom-made T-shirts for the occasion, complete with their names and job titles for the “Dolly Department Company”.

His is “director of hair and volume”, while his partner, Scott, is “chief vibes officer”. The pair travelled from Sydney with Lucas’ sister and her two children.

“We decided literally a year ago to all come along together … but it’s even more special now after her passing to be able to come and celebrate,” Lucas says.

“I’m sure there’ll be many drinks and many sing-alongs tonight. It’s the soul behind her songs we love – just warming and inclusive .”

An eclectic cast of Dollys

Soon, darkness will descend, lipstick will smudge and cowboy hats may be lost. But first, a best-dressed winner must be crowned. And who better to lead the proceedings than the drag queen Timberlina, who grew up in regional New South Wales and has emceed the festival for the past five years.

In true Dolly fashion, she arrives in a vintage car and snatched rainbow dress, waving regally.

Children are judged first, then comes the best-dressed Kenny, a homage to Parton’s longtime collaborator Kenny Rogers. There are three finalists, including a man dressed as Woody from Toy Story.

Then the Dollys flock to the red carpet, as diverse and eclectic as the singer’s own career. One woman rides a blow-up horse. A small child somehow makes her way on to the stage. Fake breasts jut out of tight dresses like bowling balls waiting to be freed.

Dolly Delicious, sporting her victory sash from 2023, slowly walks among them, eventually landing on Colin Marshall – who is part of a tour group of 30 people who have travelled to Narromine from Brisbane. The tour is run by Fun Over 50 Holidays, and he isn’t the only man who has come in drag.

“It wasn’t just the look, it was the warmth, the attitude,” Dolly Delicious tells the crowd. Marshall booms: “Over 50s!”

His wife, Leanne, crafted his outfit. He is wearing a hot pink tasselled dress, a blond wig, a cowboy hat, heels and large sunglasses, and accepts his sash as though it’s an inevitability.

For a full minute, Marshall sashays along the runway, swinging his arms with abandon. I ask him how it feels to win. “Good, great,” he replies.

“It’s hard work being a woman.”

article_text:
No one is ever upset, or even disappointed, when Sir Patrick Stewart pops up onscreen. Whether he’s the umpteenth cameo in a Marvel movie or a surprise addition to a sprawling Super Bowl commercial , the master of Shakespeare and generational captain is always greeted by audiences with eager anticipation, if not outright glee.

But Stewart, who died Thursday afternoon from Alzheimer’s disease and Lewy body dementia, didn’t treat his warm regard as a given. He saw the respect he earned throughout his towering career as an opportunity for what to do next — not for easy paychecks from familiar parts, but to push himself into new territory and delight audiences all over again.

Perhaps that’s why when I heard of his passing, my first memory was from one of his lesser-seen roles. “ Blunt Talk ” was a hot commodity when Starz picked it up in 2014. Seth MacFarlane (who worked with Stewart on “Family Guy,” “American Dad,” and “Ted”) was producing, and Stewart was starring as a past-his-prime British news anchor attempting to start anew in America. The premium cable network gave the comedy, from “Bored to Death” creator Jonathan Ames, a straight-to-series order with a two-season commitment.

And that’s exactly how long it lasted: two, 10-episode seasons, neither of which earned the acclaim or viewership the network expected. Stewart snagged a Golden Globe nomination (his last of three total, following nods for the 2005 TV remake of “The Lion in the Winter” and 1999’s two-episode “Moby Dick” adaptation), but reviews were middling and interest fell off quickly.

I’ll admit: I don’t remember much of the show’s plot, in part because it wasn’t as “grand” as I initially thought . Stewart’s character, Walter Blunt, was a handful — only understood by his trusty valet (Adrian Scarborough), a fellow veteran of the Falklands War, and constantly challenged by his staff, producers, and studio executives. The stubborn lost soul ended up in one preposterous situation after the next, a comedic version of the era’s antihero obsession: a drunk womanizer who virtually no one liked, clinging onto what little respect he had left.

But Stewart was having a ball. He said as much during the show’s press tour, which means next to nothing, but he backed it up in every scene, no matter how ridiculous, no matter how awkward, no matter how trivial. There’s a meta joy to his inebriated Shakespeare riff from the top of a cop car in the premiere. There’s relatable hilarity to his embarrassing battle with no-touch appliances in an airport restroom. There’s pitying chuckles to his childlike dependence on his peculiarly loyal man servant.

Frankly, Stewart brings so much to a series that never lives up to his offerings, but he and it become all the more endearing for the same reason. It would be simple to say “Blunt Talk” left a mark because Stewart got to play outside of his comfort zone; he delighted in subverting the expectations attached to a captain, a professor, and a two-time Olivier Award winner (not to mention a man whose natural baritone commanded gravitas with every syllable), and what few folks who watched him do it got to share in his delight.

But I think why Stewart’s performance in “Blunt Talk” surpasses any other memory of the series — and briefly surpassed any other memory I had of an actor who could do anything (and saw everything ) — is because it exemplifies his unique, enduring blend of affability and ability. Patrick was an actor we never tired of seeing (or hearing), even when we had ample reason to assume we’d seen (or heard) this before.

As Picard, Stewart logged well over 200 episodes and led four movies. He revived Charles Xavier across nearly a dozen films (including the upcoming “Avengers: Doomsday”). He voiced Deputy Director Avery Bullock in 125 episodes of “American Dad” (a role he cited as his favorite voice-acting performance ). He brought in audiences night after night to see his one-man-show of “A Christmas Carol,” his Tony Award-nominated work in “Macbeth,” and his heralded performances in “The Tempest,” “The Ride Down Mt. Morgan,” “Who’s Afraid of Virginia Woolf?”, “Antony and Cleopatra,” and “Hamlet.”

His lifetime of work should feel like plenty, and instead it feels like barely enough. Even his lesser projects now seem like they deserved more. That’s the level of care he brought to the screen, and it’s partly why he’ll be so missed from future screenings.

Sir Patrick Stewart was a man who was easy to like and an actor who was easy to admire. He never took either for granted. Thankfully, we never took him for granted either.
