title_original: Archives : The Music Photography Gallery : Interview with Bob Gruen
editorial_title_zh: 档案：“音乐摄影画廊”：鲍勃·格鲁恩访谈
editorial_excerpt_zh: 档案 – 2025年10月22日 鲍勃·格鲁恩是音乐摄影界的标志性人物。尽管他作为约翰·列农的摄影师而闻名于世——他捕捉了 […] 这篇题为“档案：“音乐摄影画廊”：鲍勃·格鲁恩访谈”的文章最先发布在《摄影之眼》……
editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "档案 – 2025年10月22日", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "鲍勃·格鲁恩（Bob Gruen）是音乐摄影界的标志性人物。尽管他作为约翰·列农（John Lennon）的摄影师而世界闻名——他在1974年捕捉到了这位音乐家在纽约天际线前的传奇松弛感——但他首先是整个摇滚乐坛的肖像摄影师，见证了摇滚乐在1970年代的爆发。几十年来，他一直在单一座右铭的指引下捕捉这种独特的能量：自由。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "他和画廊主塞巴斯蒂安·阿尔德雷特（Sebastian Alderete）的相遇，为他打开通往艺术摄影这个有时极其专属的世界的大门。阿尔德雷特通过“音乐摄影画廊”（The Music Photography Gallery）充满激情地致力于提高音乐摄影的认可度，该画廊将自己定位为唯一一家致力于推广原作印相（vintage prints）的画廊，而原作印相是让这一长期代表性不足的流派获得认可的核心要素：“收购一张原作印相，就是收购一个时刻，一段对时间中独一无二时刻的回忆。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "从这个意义上说，鲍勃·格鲁恩的收藏是一个真正的宝库，其中包含他早在1960年代就在暗室中亲自制作的印相——银盐印相、威发相纸（Cibachromes）、宝丽来（Polaroids）——所有这些都得到了完美的保存，并且是最早制作的音乐摄影实体印相之一。自2016年以来，“音乐摄影画廊”一直与大约20位摄影师共同代表这批作品，其中包括米克·洛克（Mick Rock）、罗伯塔·贝利（Roberta Bayley）、玛西亚·雷斯尼克（Marcia Resnick）和丹尼尔·克雷默（Daniel Kramer）——塞巴斯蒂安·阿尔德雷特正是通过鲍勃·格鲁恩结识了他们。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "今天，这位备受推崇的摇滚摄影师向《摄影之眼》（L’Œil de la Photographie）分享了他的创作历程与摄影愿景。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "鲍勃·格鲁恩，你是如何成为一名音乐摄影师的？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我很小的时候就跟母亲学习摄影。她是一名律师，但她的业余爱好是摄影。她自己冲洗并印制照片。我不到5岁时，她就建了一个暗室并把我带了进去。我着迷于在暗室的空白纸张上看着一张照片显影的过程。我在8岁时得到了第一台相机。到了11岁时，我已经在夏令营里拍照，然后把胶卷寄回家给我母亲，她把冲好的照片寄回来，我再把它们卖给营员。基本上从那时起我一直都在做这件事，只不过我妈妈不再帮我冲印了。高中毕业后，我尝试了几所对我来说并不适合的大学，于是我听从了蒂莫西·利里（Timothy Leary）的建议：“开启、合拍、离去”（turn on, tune in, and drop out）。我辍学去和一个摇滚乐队生活在一起，他们是我高中的朋友，我开始为他们拍照。当他们拿到唱片合约时，唱片公司注意到了我，并开始雇我去拍其他工作。事情就这样一环扣一环地发展下去了……", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这一切真正开始于1970年，多亏了蒂娜·特纳（Tina Turner）。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "是的，就在那一年的夏天。我们的一个朋友叫我去看看艾克与蒂娜·特纳（Ike and Tina Turner）的演出。她的表演彻底震撼了我。几天后我又去了，这次带上了我的相机。这是我第一次拍摄我不认识的人，而不是我的朋友。那天晚上我拍了一些照片，其中有一张特别好，是她在频闪灯下跳着离开舞台的照片。相机里还剩几帧，我想也许我可以把相机打开一秒钟，在闪烁的灯光下捕捉几张蒂娜的影像。冲洗出来的其中一张照片绝对完美。它被拿来与杜尚（Duchamp）的《下楼梯的裸女》（1912）相提并论，因为它是蒂娜的五张影像以某种方式相互重叠。这不是Photoshop。这是一张曝光一秒钟的照片。它确实捕捉到了蒂娜·特纳所具有的所有激动与能量。几天后，我们又去看他们的演出，一个朋友硬把我推到了艾克·特纳（Ike Turner）面前。他看了看照片，非常喜欢。几天后在纽约，他把我介绍给唱片公司的一位公关，后者带我去参加了一个派对，在那里我遇到了另外两位公关。其中一位雇我去拍埃尔顿·约翰（Elton John），然后就像滚雪球一样停不下来了。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这也促成了你在1971年于比肯剧院（Beacon Theatre）举办的首次摄影展，这是一场具有里程碑意义的展览，当音乐摄影仅通过专辑封面或杂志为人所知时，它将音乐摄影挂上了墙壁。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我遇到了一位在比肯剧院制作音乐会的演出商。她非常希望能联系到艾克与蒂娜·特纳，于是我把她引荐给艾克，他们举办了一场大型音乐会。为了报答我，她帮我制作了一整套30乘40英寸的印相，并将其包裹在硬质纤维板（masonite）上，这是一种非常独特的工艺，只有我合作过的那家冲印厂才能制作。那个人能够制作一张30乘40英寸的大幅印相，在它仍然湿润的时候，把它包裹在一块类似木头、厚约四分之一英寸的硬质纤维板上。这样一来，它们就变成了一块坚固厚重的展板。我把它们挂在比肯剧院里，这基本上就是我的首个个人展览。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "使用大幅印相是将音乐摄影引入艺术领域的一种方式。你曾经与这个摄影界有过联系吗？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我与这个圈子其实并没有太多交集。在1970年代的某个时候，我曾受邀参加阿尔勒摄影节（Rencontres d’Arles）。当时我并不真正理解去那里参会和结识同行有多么重要，我真的很天真。我有些后悔错过了那个深入了解摄影艺术界的机会，因为我一直觉得我想成为其中一部分，却从未真正建立起联系。每当我去看这类展览时，我都觉得那些影像要沉静得多。而我的作品充满声响，那是摇滚乐的声音。正因如此，我总是使用大尺寸照片：它们必须足够喧闹。我想这在摄影界曾显得有些离经叛道。当然，情况正在发生变化，我很幸运能让自己的作品在巴黎摄影展（Paris Photo）、伦敦摄影展（Photo London）及同类艺博会上展出。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "你觉得你的照片有何不同之处？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我有一种天赋，能拍出不流于俗套肖像的人物佳作。自从我懂事起，我的人生目标、我的人生主题就是自由。我13岁时看的第一场演唱会是皮特·西格（Pete Seeger）的演出。我记得他谈到了个人自由、平等权利之类的话题。我总是倾向于带有某种讯息的音乐。鲍勃·迪伦（Bob Dylan）、纽约玩偶乐队（New York Dolls）、冲撞乐队（The Clash），或是后来的绿日乐队（Green Day）：这些人都在用摇滚乐表明立场。对我而言，摇滚乐关乎自由，关乎在公众面前大声表达真实感受的自由。它关乎那种所有人都在尖叫、没人去想交房租的时刻。我一直试图在照片中捕捉这种感觉。我最喜欢听到的赞美之一，就是人们看到我的照片时说，他们几乎能听见声音。这就是我一直在努力做的，我试图捕捉身临其境的感觉。正因如此，我一直认为它更接近艺术，而不仅仅是新闻。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "看你的摄影作品，也会让人觉得你所提及的那种自由似乎早已一去不复返了。随着音乐产业和商业演出的崛起，如今的音乐人或其他名人对自身形象的掌控度极高。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "是的，现在一切都受到更多控制了。在80年代，当各大企业看到音乐产业有利可图时，情况就变了。它们开始试图进行更多的控制。你必须签署合同，规定你只能拍摄某些特定的照片。你知道的，滚石杂志（Rolling Stone）直到1967年左右才创刊，奶油杂志（Cream）也差不多在那个时候问世。当时并没有太多的媒体。摇滚乐队根本进不了纽约时报（The New York Times），甚至连纽约邮报（New York Post）也进不去。在70年代，人们一听说你要拍他们的照片并刊登在杂志上，会感到兴奋不已。而如今他们经常受到评论，他们已是文化的一部分，但在当年，选择摇滚乐依然会被视作你在接触某种不良音乐。我记得这一切刚开始的时候，人们常常说“这阵风会过去，这不重要”。但它确实重要，因为它是一种能够启发人们心智的自由节奏。而且它已经传遍了全世界。它现在已然成为了世界的语言。这让我觉得很有意思，因为事实证明，我当时确实在记录一种文化。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "你当时敏锐捕捉到的另一件事是照片冲印件的重要性。你至今仍保留着那个时代令人惊叹的老照片原件。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我一直拥有自己的暗房，并亲自冲洗照片。很多其他摄影师不得不把胶片送去冲印店制作，那代价不菲。所以他们通常只会制作一两张照片送去杂志社。我总是会多洗几张照片。你知道的，我一生中只上过两门课，是在纽约摄影时装学院（Fashion Institute of Photography）学的。那是我受过的仅有的正规摄影培训。我在那里从一位教授身上学到的一点是，每当你冲洗照片时，一定要洗两到三张，因为你冲洗这张照片的唯一原因就是有人喜欢它，而你接下来是要把它送人的。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "但如果你没有实体冲印件，你就等于没有照片。所以我总是多冲洗一些照片，现在我手里还留存着许多追溯到50年或60年前的老照片。事实证明，如今老照片原件有着巨大的市场。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "你最著名的照片之一是你在纽约天际线前拍摄的约翰·列农（John Lennon）。但如果你能在作为音乐摄影师的职业生涯中创作的大量作品里挑选一张，你会选哪一张？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "嗯，这就好比让我选出自己最喜欢的孩子。我有很多喜欢的作品，当然包括我前面提到的那张蒂娜·特纳（Tina Turner）的照片，也包括好几张约翰·列农的照片。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "不仅仅是那张纽约城市的照片。更重要的是我在自由女神像前为他拍的那张。那是少数几张我提前构思过的照片。我通常不会刻意去计划我的拍摄。我通常只是走到拍摄对象所在的地方，非常自然地抓拍一张他在那个空间里的好照片。但对于那一张……当时约翰·列农正遭到政府起诉。他们想把他驱逐出境。我觉得自由女神像是欢迎的绝佳象征。我们本该欢迎像约翰·列农这样的人。我向他提了这个建议，他很喜欢这个想法。他对媒体有着高度的敏感，并且深谙这样一张照片的力量。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我们去了那里，过程非常简单。我们俩只是坐了渡轮，在自由女神像前拍了几张照片。自从他去世后，那张照片便被赋予了更多的含义，因为我认为约翰·列农和自由女神像都代表着个人自由。就像我所说的那样，这是我一生的主题。所以我不得不说，那是我的最爱之一。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "采访：佐伊·伊尔·德·博沙讷（Zoé Isle de Beauchaine）", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The Music Photo Gallery TMPG [ 仅限预约 ] 118 S 3rd St. Brooklyn, NY 11249 www.musicphoto.net", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "www.bobgruen.com", "translated": true}]
article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "Archives – October 22, 2025"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Bob Gruen is an icon of music photography. While he is world-famous as John Lennon ’ s photographer — capturing the musician ’ s legendary nonchalance in front of the New York skyline in 1974 — he is above all the portraitist of the entire rock and roll scene, which he witnessed erupt in the 1970s. For decades, he has captured this unique energy, guided by a single motto: freedom."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "His encounter with gallery owner Sebastian Alderete opened the doors to a sometimes very exclusive world, that of art photography. Alderete works passionately to promote greater recognition of music photography through the Music Photography Gallery, which positions itself as the only gallery dedicated to the valorisation of vintage prints, an essential factor in gaining recognition for this still underrepresented genre: « A cquiring a vintage print is acquiring a moment, the recollection of a unique moment in time. »"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "In this sense, Bob Gruen ’ s collection is a true treasure, made up of prints he produced himself in his darkroom as early as the 1960s — silver prints, Cibachromes, Polaroids — all perfectly preserved and amongst the first physical prints ever made of music photography. Since 2016, the Music Photography Gallery has represented this body of work alongside about twenty photographers, including Mick Rock, Roberta Bayley, Marcia Resnick, and Daniel Kramer — whom Sebastian Alderete met through Bob Gruen."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Today, f or L ’Œ il de la Photographie, the most regarded rock and roll photographer shares the story of his journey and his vision of photography."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Bob Gruen, h ow did you become a music photographer?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "I learned photography from my mother when I was very little. She was an attorney, but her hobby was photography. She developed and printed her own pictures. When I was less than five years old, she built a darkroom and took me in. article_text:
Archives – October 22, 2025

Bob Gruen is an icon of music photography. While he is world-famous as John Lennon ’ s photographer — capturing the musician ’ s legendary nonchalance in front of the New York skyline in 1974 — he is above all the portraitist of the entire rock and roll scene, which he witnessed erupt in the 1970s. For decades, he has captured this unique energy, guided by a single motto: freedom.

His encounter with gallery owner Sebastian Alderete opened the doors to a sometimes very exclusive world, that of art photography. Alderete works passionately to promote greater recognition of music photography through the Music Photography Gallery, which positions itself as the only gallery dedicated to the valorisation of vintage prints, an essential factor in gaining recognition for this still underrepresented genre: « A cquiring a vintage print is acquiring a moment, the recollection of a unique moment in time. »

In this sense, Bob Gruen ’ s collection is a true treasure, made up of prints he produced himself in his darkroom as early as the 1960s — silver prints, Cibachromes, Polaroids — all perfectly preserved and amongst the first physical prints ever made of music photography. Since 2016, the Music Photography Gallery has represented this body of work alongside about twenty photographers, including Mick Rock, Roberta Bayley, Marcia Resnick, and Daniel Kramer — whom Sebastian Alderete met through Bob Gruen.

Today, f or L ’Œ il de la Photographie, the most regarded rock and roll photographer shares the story of his journey and his vision of photography.

Bob Gruen, h ow did you become a music photographer?

I learned photography from my mother when I was very little. She was an attorney, but her hobby was photography. She developed and printed her own pictures. When I was less than five years old, she built a darkroom and took me in. I was fascinated with the process of watching a photo develop on a blank piece of paper in a darkroom. I got my first camera when I was eight years old. By the time I was 11, I was taking pictures at summer camp and I would send the film home to my mother, she’d send prints back which I then sold to the campers.That’s basically what I’ve been doing ever since, except my mom doesn’t print for me anymore. After high school, I tried a couple of colleges that didn’t really work for me so I took Timothy Leary’s advice to « turn on, tune in, and drop out. » I dropped out to live with a rock and roll band, friends of mine from high school and I started started taking pictures of them. When they got a record contract, the record company found out about me and started to hire me for other jobs. And one thing led to another…

It all really started in 1970, thanks to Tina Turner.

Yes, in the summer of that year. A friend of ours told me to go see Ike and Tina Turner. I was totally blown away by her performance. I came back a couple of days later, this time with my camera. It was the first time I photographed somebody I didn’t know, and not my friends. I took some pictures that night and one was especially good, of her dancing off the stage to a strobe light. I had a few frames left in the camera and I thought that maybe if I would open the camera for one second to catch a couple of images of Tina in the flashing lights. One of the resulting images is absolutely perfect. It has been compared to Duchamp’s Nude Descending a Staircase (1912) because it’s five images of Tina kind of overlapping each other. It’s not Photoshop. It’s a one-second picture. It really captures all the excitement and energy that is Tina Turner. A few days later we went back to their show and a friend literally pushed me in front of Ike Turner. He looked at the pictures and liked them a lot. A couple of days later in New York, he introduced me to a publicist at a record company who took me to a party where I met two other publicists. One of them hired me to shoot Elton John, and then the snowball just started rolling.

This also led to your first photography exhibition at the Beacon Theatre in 1971, a landmark show that put music photography on the walls when it was only known through album covers or magazines.

I met a promoter who was putting on concerts at the Beacon Theatre. She was very excited to get in touch with Ike and Tina Turner so I introduced her to Ike and they played a big concert. To pay me back, she helped me produce a whole set of 30 by 40 prints that I made wrapped around masonite, which was a very unique process that only this lab I worked with could make. The guy was able to make a big 30 by 40 print and while it was still wet, he would wrap it around a piece of masonite, which is like wood and about a quarter of an inch thick. That way they would become a solid heavy panel. I put them up in the Beacon Theatre, which was basically my very first exhibition.

Using large prints was a way to introduce music photography into the realm of art. Did you ever have a link with this photography scene ?

I was not very connected to this scene. I was invited at one point in the 1970s to be part of the Rencontres d’Arles in Arles. And back then I didn’t really understand the importance of going there and meet people. I was really naive. I regret that I missed that moment to learn more about the art world of photography because I’ve always felt that I wanted to be part of that, but I never really had the connection. When I go to these kind of shows I find the images much calmer. My work is loud, it’s the sound of rock and roll. That’s why I was always using big prints : they had to be loud. And I think that was kind of shocking for the photography world. Things are changing of course and I was lucky to have my pictures shown in Paris Photo, Photo London and similar fairs.

What do you think was different about your pictures ?

I had a talent to take good pictures of people that was not just pleasing portraits. Ever since I grew up, my goal, my theme in life has been freedom. My first concert when I was 13 was Pete Seeger. I remember he talked about personal freedom and equal rights and things like that. I always lean towards music with a message. Bob Dylan, the New York Dolls, The Clash, or later Green Day : these people are using rock and roll to make a statement. To me, rock and roll is about freedom, it’s about the freedom to express your feelings very loudly in public. It’s about that moment when everybody’s screaming and nobody’s thinking about paying the rent. I’ve always tried to catch that feeling in the pictures. One of my favorite compliments is that people see my pictures, they say they can practically hear it. That’s what I’m trying to do, I’m trying to capture the feeling of being there. That’s why I’ve always thought of it more about art and not just journalism.

Looking at your photography, there is also a feeling that the freedom you mention seems long gone. With the rise of the industry, show business, nowadays musicians or other celebrities are very much in control of their image.

Yes, everything is much more controlled now. In the 80s when the corporations started seeing that there was money in the music business, things changed. They started trying to control things a lot more. You had to sign a contract that you could only take certain pictures. You know, Rolling Stone only started around 1967 and Cream magazine around the same time. There wasn’t a lot of media back then. Rock and roll bands did not get into the New York Times or even the New York Post. In the 70s, people were thrilled that you would take their picture because and put them in a magazine. Nowadays they get reviewed regularly, they are part of the culture but at the time, choosing rock and roll was still deemed that you went on delinquent music. I remember when it all started people used to say « it’s going to pass, it’s not important. » But it is important because it’s a rhythm of freedom that opens people up. And it’s spread around the world. It’s the language of the world now. It’s interesting to me because it turned out I was actually capturing a culture.

Another thing you sensed at the time was the importance of prints. You still have incredible vintage prints from that time.

I’ve always had my own darkroom and made my own prints. A lot of other photographers had to go to labs and have them made, and that would be expensive. So they would only have one or two prints made that they would send to a magazine. I always had extra prints made. You know, I only took two classes in my life, at the Fashion Institute of Photography. That’s the only formal photography training I’ve had. One of the things I learned from the professor there was that whenever you’re making a print, always make two or three, because the only reason you’re making the print is because somebody liked that photo and you’re going to give it away.

But if you don’t have a print, you don’t have a photo. So I always made extra prints and I have lots of them now that dates back to 50 or 60 years ago. And it turned out that there is a big market for the vintage print today.

O ne of your most famous pictures is the one you took of John Lennon in front of New York’s skyline. But if you could choose one pictures amongst the many you have produced throughout your career as a music photographer, which one would it be ?

Well, this is like asking for my favorite child. I have a lot of favorites, certainly the Tina Turner picture I mentioned earlier but also certainly several pictures of John Lennon.

Not just the New York City picture. Even more important is the picture I took of him at the Statue of Liberty. That’s one of the few pictures that I thought of in advance. I don’t usually plan my pictures.I usually just go wherever the subject is and try to get a good picture of him in that space very spontaneously. But for that one… John Lennon was being charged by the government. They wanted to deport him and send him out of the country. I felt that the Statue of Liberty was a good symbol of welcome. We should be welcoming people like John Lennon. I suggested it to him, he liked the idea. He was very aware of the media and he understood the power of a picture like that.

We went out there, it was just very simple. The two of us just took the ferry and took a couple of pictures in front of the Statue of Liberty. That picture has taken on a lot more meaning since he passed away, because I think that John Lennon and the Statue of Liberty both represent personal freedom. And like I said, that’s been my theme all my life. So I would have to say that’s one of my favorites.

Interview by Zoé Isle de Beauchaine

article_text:
Get used to seeing these faces this awards season. Variety’s 2026 10 Actors to Watch took the stage in Newport Beach, California, for a conversation about performance, craft and process on October 18. Variety moderated this conversation in partnership with Newport Beach Film Festival .

The panel kicked off at the Balboa Bay Resort, highlighting this year’s selection: Jaafar Jackson (“Michael”), Inde Navarrette (“Obsession”), Ray Nicholson (“The Mosquito Bowl”), Esmé Creed-Miles (“Sense and Sensibility”), Mariana Di Girólamo (“Wild Horse Nine”), Rosalind Eleazar (“Misty Green”), Guitarricadelafuente (“La Bola Negra”), Summer H. Howell (“Carrie”), Ruth Madeley (“Being Heumann”) and Joseph Zada (“The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping”).

Related Stories

Connor Storrie in Talks to Play Villain Opposite Ryan Gosling in Marvel's 'Ghost Rider'

'The Notebook' Musical Sets West End Run at Newly Renamed Judi Dench Theatre

During the conversation, Navarrette opened up about portraying Nikki and the challenge of developing a character since there is so little of the real Nikki in “Obsession.”

“It was really just my first opportunity where I kind of had the freedom, to a certain extent, to do whatever I could,” she said. “I really find the complication of Nikki to be what is the most beautiful about her. And I find people come up and they talk to me about her — specifically women — say, ‘That is a character that I find myself in.’ Of course people like to laugh, but I find that there’s a complexity, not just in women, but in us as people, where we are multiple people, and that’s beautiful.”

Jackson also spoke about the process of becoming his uncle, Michael Jackson , not just in his skills as a performer but also in his confidence.

“I just wanted it to come across as I’ve done films before. I didn’t want to be seen as a first-time actor. I wanted to be able to, of course, continue to learn, but have that presence and awareness of how to walk into a room, how to get pulled in any direction because it doesn’t always go as planned or what’s on the page,” he said. “Something can happen the day of, and I was experiencing that, and I was glad I was able to prep for that and just to be in that space where Michael would do it, just to continue to be in the mind of Michael.

Watch part one of the video above and part two below:

article_text:
Ever since Daniel Craig announced that he would be turning in the tuxedo and putting down the martini glass, the race has been on to decide who will be chosen as the next James Bond. The rumor mill has been heating up for years now, but now it’s really down to the wire for the final weeks of auditions for Bond 26. With stories dropping daily about who Bond producers are meeting with, fans are hoping it might soon be revealed who will take over as Ian Fleming’s iconic character.

Once “Dune” director Denis Villeneuve was hired to shepherd the next installment, with Steven Knight writing the script, it was off to the races to decide who casting director Nina Gold and Villeneuve would select.

Here’s what we do know: The new Bond will almost certainly not be the familiar 007. If the next film follows the timeline of “No Time to Die,” then James Bond is dead and Lashana Lynch’s character Nomi adopted his MI6 agent number. Of course, the next Bond movie could easily set that established timeline aside, and take place in an alternate Bond universe altogether. (It never made much sense that Sean Connery’s Bond from the 1960s and Pierce Brosnan’s Bond from the 1990s were the same person, anyway.)

The series’ previous producers Barbara Broccoli and Michael Wilson were clear about three things: The next Bond should be played by a Brit; the next Bond should be young enough to be able to continue in the role for at least 15 years; and the next Bond will be a man, not a woman.

But with Broccoli and Wilson turning over creative control to Amazon MGM, there’s no telling what changes might be in store. Amy Pascal and David Heyman are now producing, and since it’s their first Bond film, any number of changes could be in store. And as Agent 007 knows better than most, rules are meant to be bent, if not broken outright.

For this list, we cast a wide net of actors mostly in the under-40 category — yes, even a couple of women — so sorry to earlier picks like Idris Elba, Henry Cavill and others who have aged out of the running. The most important criteria was whether the actor could bring the necessary gravitas, style and charm to playing Britain’s most famous secret agent.

While awaiting the next Bond to be cast, catch up by watching all the Bond films in order .

(Contributors: Pat Saperstein, Rachel Seo, William Earl, J. Kim Murphy, Jenelle Riley, Caroline Framke, Jordan Moreau, Michaela Zee, EJ Panaligan, Katie Reul, Ellise Shafer, Maane Khatchatourian, Adam B. Vary, Ethan Shanfeld, Andrés Buenahora, Angelique Jackson, Jack Dunn)

Callum Turner Image Credit: Getty Images Before appearing in “Eternity” and “Rosebush Pruning,” Callum Turner led the helm in the sports drama “The Boys in The Boat.” And while rowing may have sharpened his look and physicality, playing an athlete is far from the only thing he can do. In addition to playing a likable suitor to Anya Taylor-Joy in the 2020 screen adaptation of Jane Austen’s “Emma,” the London-born actor has appeared in a diverse slate of films, from the video game-to-film adaptation “Assassin’s Creed” to the Harry Potter-universe’s “Fantastic Beasts: The Crimes of Grindelwald.” He also starred as Maj. John ‘Bucky’ Egan opposite Austin Butler in the Steven Spielberg-executive produced “Masters of The Air.” The Apple TV+ miniseries displayed his capacity for aerial combat scenes, which could bode exceptionally well for any potential Bond films that require 007 to jump out of a moving plane or perform any flying stunts in debonair fashion.

Jack Lowden Image Credit: Getty Images A ginger James Bond? Stranger things have happened. The Scottish actor has been winning acclaim as River Cartwright in the popular spy series “Slow Horses,” and will soon show his romantic side as Mr. Darcy in Netflix’s “Pride & Prejudice” series. Beyond that, he’s built up a solid list of credits over the years. From Steve McQueen’s “Small Axe” to Christopher Nolan’s “Dunkirk” to the action-packed series “The Tunnel,” Lowden has taken on numerous dramatic and stunt-filled roles that could help pave the way for playing Bond.

Josh O’Connor Image Credit: Getty Images Born in Cheltenham, Josh O’Connor appeared in “Les Miserables” and “The Durrells” before gaining international recognition and winning the Emmy as Prince Charles in “The Crown.” O’Connor also made an impression as a raffish Italian-speaking antiquities thief in Alice Rohrwacher’s “La Chimera” before getting into the game as part of the sexy tennis playing-trio in Luca Guadagnino’s “Challengers.” He certainly showed off his sex appeal as part of the audacious triangle, but does he have the action attitude needed to play 007?

Jack O’Connell Image Credit: Getty Images Already the winner of a BAFTA Award, an Actor Award and a Gotham Award, the “Sinners” and “28 Years Later” actor was born in Albaston, Derbyshire. O’Connell tangled with the law as a teenager and came to audiences’ attention as a young delinquent in “Skins,” later channelling his father’s Irish heritage as the musical vampire in “Sinners.” The question is, can an actor known for his intensity playing criminals and broken men smooth off his angry persona to play the suave spy? His recent roles in films like “Ink” show there’s more range than his early string of bad boys.

Jacob Elordi Image Credit: Dave Benett/Getty Images for TAG After Craig’s 15-year-long tenure, young people need a Bond to call their own — and it’s high time to return 007 to his roots as a professional, debonair psychopath. Who better for that than Elordi, the hunky 6’5’’ Aussie — still the Commonwealth! — who added an unmistakable menace to “Euphoria” and “The Kissing Booth” trilogy. From the enigmatic Creature in “Frankenstein” to the dashing Heathcliff in “Wuthering Heights,” Elordi certainly has the range to embody all the facets of the Bond character.

Aaron Taylor-Johnson Image Credit: Dave J Hogan/Getty Images Beyond the charm, Bond is an adrenaline junkie with destructive and promiscuous tendencies — a role that British actor Taylor-Johnson certainly knows how to fill following his 2016 performance as villain Ray Marcus in the psychological thriller “Nocturnal Animals.” Taylor-Johnson’s execution of the part landed him a nomination for best supporting actor at the BAFTAs that same year. The star is also known to audiences as Dave Lizewski in the action-comedy “Kick-Ass,” Pietro Maximoff in Marvel’s “Avengers: Age of Ultron” and a wise-cracking hitman in “Bullet Train.” His breadth is proof that the malleable actor can handle both the dark, justice-hungry and quick-witted, idealistic sides of 007.

Harris Dickinson Image Credit: Gilbert Flores Harris Dickinson acted as eye candy for Nicole Kidman in “Babygirl,” but the 30-year-old offers a more nuanced range than fans may realize. The Essex-born actor possesses the charisma and suave factor to take up the mantle of James Bond, having played an insecure male model and influencer in the Oscar-nominated “Triangle of Sadness” and a golden boy in the screen adaptation of Delia Owens’ original novel “Where The Crawdads Sing.” Furthermore, the physicality he displayed as a professional wrestler opposite Zac Efron and Jeremy Allen White in “The Iron Claw” could enhance his adaptability to high-intensity action sequences and combat aspects necessary for the role of 007.

Regé-Jean Page Image Credit: Getty Images for Lexus The “Bridgerton” breakout first stirred Bond suspicions when he tweeted “Regency, royalty. Shaken and stirred” before the wildly popular Netflix series’ Season 1 premiere. Since then, he’s acquired a fan base who would love to see him as the next 007. With his dashing good looks and charming delivery, there’s no doubt Page would make a fantastic Bond – and he would bring some much-overdue diversity to the franchise. Though he proved his status as a heartthrob in “Bridgerton,” he’s also sharpened his action chops, having starred in Netflix’s popular “The Gray Man.” What’s more, his career has just started to take shape over the last few years, putting him in that sweet spot between unknown and superstar that could make for a long and fruitful Bond run.

Paul Mescal Image Credit: Stuart C. Wilson/Getty Images Born in County Kildare, Ireland, Paul Mescal was a high-scoring soccer player in his younger days, which should help with the athleticism a new James Bond would require. He first came to prominence with his role in “Normal People,” which garnered him an Emmy nom and made him a romantic role model. The Oscar-nominated actor displayed his action chops in “Gladiator II” and won acclaim in “Hamnet.” Before the opening of the Ridley Scott epic, “Spectre” actor Andrew Scott talked to Variety about Mescal playing 007, saying: “He’d probably be a great James Bond.”

Tom Francis Image Credit: Getty Images With baby blue eyes and a classic British charm, Tom Francis could complete his leap from the stage to the screen with Bond. In fact, Variety even reported back in May that he had auditioned to be the next 007. The 27-year-old Suffolk native is mainly known for this theater work, including starring opposite Nicole Scherzinger in Jamie Lloyd’s “Sunset Boulevard,” which earned him both a Tony nomination and Olivier Award. However, he’s been slowly making a name in the film world, appearing in “Jay Kelly” alongside George Clooney and starring in Peter Berg’s war drama “The Mosquito Bowl.” Francis might just be the perfect newcomer to make the spy franchise his calling card — plus, have you seen him shirtless (and covered in blood) during the “Sunset Boulevard” bows?!

Damson Idris Image Credit: Getty Images “Snowfall” actor Damson Idris was at one time rumored to have auditioned for the Bond producers. Bookmakers in the U.K. were quick to put him near the top of the list of Bond prospects when the news of the purported audition came out. The actor was born in London to Nigerian parents, and started his career acting onstage before getting playing Franklin Saint, an American drug dealer, in the series “Snowfall.” He went on to appear in shows such as “Black Mirror” and “Swarm.” An experienced football and rugby player, he also showed his driving skills in “F1” and his athletic background could be an asset during rigorous action sequences.

Nicholas Hoult Image Credit: Stephane Cardinale - Corbis/Corbis via Getty Images With his piercing blue eyes and boyish charm, Nicholas Hoult has been a heartthrob since his days as Tony Stonem in the British dramedy series “Skins.” The actor has proven his versatility in action films, from wielding medieval weapons in “Jack the Giant Slayer” to unleashing the mutant Beast in the “X-Men” franchise. Not to mention, Hoult has managed to woo viewers with such unlikely characters as the undead R in “Warm Bodies” and the psychotic Nux in “Mad Max: Fury Road,” so there’s no denying that “The Great” star can incorporate a similar complexity and allure to Bond.

Aaron Pierre Image Credit: Getty Images for BET Aaron Pierre might be too busy starring as John Stewart in DC’s superhero series “Lanterns” to add James Bond to his dance card, but the British star has all the necessaries to play the suave secret agent if he were to accept the mission. Standing 6-foot-3 with broad shoulders and striking hazel eyes, the Brixton native established himself as an action star with the surprise Netflix hit “Rebel Ridge,” where he showed off his martial arts, boxing and Brazilian Jujitsu skills. And he’s got brains to go with all that brawn. Pierre is a classically trained actor (an alum of the London Academy of Music and Dramatic Art) and his performance as Cassio in “Othello” helped him land a key role in Barry Jenkins’ historical drama “The Underground Railroad.” Plus, he’s proven that he’s got the chops to play an icon: he portrayed legendary civil rights activist Malcolm X in NatGeo’s “Genius: MLK/X.” He put his rich baritone to masterful use as Mufasa in Disney’s “The Lion King” prequel.

Henry Golding Image Credit: WireImage The “Crazy Rich Asians” breakout has already proven himself to be everything Bond should be – British, dashing and in on the joke. In a short time, Golding has shown that he is not only a deft actor in a hit rom-com, but adept with thrillers (“A Simple Favor”) and action (“The Gentlemen,” “Snake Eyes.”) And for those who feel Bond has gotten far too serious, Golding can also bring a charming levity to the screen – a twinkle in the eye that his best predecessors also shared.

Lucien Laviscount Image Credit: Getty Images He was Emily’s love interest in “Emily in Paris,” which brought him international attention, and then entered the conversation to select the next James Bond. British TV viewers have seen him since he was a teen in recurring roles in series like “Grange Hill,” “Waterloo Road,” “Celebrity Big Brother” and the long-running soap “Coronation Street.” In the U.S., he appeared in “Scream Queens,” “Snatch” and “Katy Keene.” Does the debonair Lancashire native have what it takes to don the Bond tuxedo? His feature roles so far have been scarce, but with charm to spare, the Daily Mail said: “Lucien ticks all of the boxes. He is a super-talented actor, is extremely handsome, and in the past 18 months has won lots of new fans since he joined ‘Emily In Paris.’ Bond bosses are already saying how you can see him in the 007 tuxedo, how dapper and fitting to the role he will look.”

Daryl McCormack Image Credit: Getty Images for Tribeca Festiva McCormack cut his teeth acting in tough guy TV shows like “Vikings” and “Peaky Blinders” before breaking out with the Sundance hit “Good Luck to You, Leo Grande.” As the eponymous gigolo, the relative newcomer showed a smoldering intensity, sensitively and skillfully showing Emma Thompson the ropes in a hotel room for the film’s entire runtime. Quickly establishing himself as a strong screen presence, the Irish actor is primed to connect with audiences in a big way — he just needs some shoes to fill. And he can easily wear Bond’s Crockett & Jones oxfords for a decade or two since he’s in his early 30s.

Joe Alwyn Image Credit: NBCU Photo Bank via Getty Images The internet’s favorite “London Boy” might have once been the plus one to the world’s biggest pop star, but Joe Alwyn’s performances as Henry Wallace in “Boy Erased” and unfaithful husband Nick in Hulu’s “Conversations With Friends” established his abilities as an actor. A spy Nick is not — but suit the Grammy Award winner up and place him in a luxe location, and it’s not hard to imagine he has a license to kill. Alwyn-as-Bond could lend a boyish, sensitive edge to the debonair super-spy.

Lashana Lynch Image Credit: Getty Images It’s a deceptively simple solution for the next Bond: Continue the story with Lashana Lynch’s character Nomi from “No Time to Die.” Her character already took up the 007 mantle from Daniel Craig’s Bond, and she proved to be a worthy, badass successor in his final outing. Lynch clearly has the action chops — look no further than her stunning turns in “The Woman King” and “Day of the Jackal.” It would be a radical passing of the torch for the franchise, but give Nomi a fresh cast of new and familiar characters and send her off on some spy adventures in the wake of Craig’s Bond’s death.

Joseph Quinn Image Credit: Getty Images If Bond producers are looking to go with a younger 007, its hard to imagine a better fit than Joseph Quinn, the Brit who became a worldwide sensation with just a handful of episodes of “Stranger Things.” After stealing every scene as Eddie Munson with pure charisma, just imagine what Quinn could do with his own franchise. By the time Bond 26 films, he will have already filmed his turn as George Harrison in the four Beatles movies and he continues to play the Human Torch in the MCU, so the question is whether the actor can move between all these worlds into Bond’s shoes.

Michaela Coel Image Credit: Getty Images The Broccoli family stated earlier they were looking for a man to fill 007’s shiny black dress shoes, but Michaela Coel would be the perfect choice for a female Bond if the new producers want to go in a different direction. The creator and star of award-winning miniseries “I May Destroy You,” the effortlessly elegant Coel also showed off her acting chops in “Black Mirror” and “The Aliens.” She also starred in “Black Panther: Wakanda Forever” and got her spy on in the “Mr. and Mrs. Smith” Amazon series. If a female Bond isn’t in the cards, maybe the next script could make room for a powerful new MI6 agent like Coel.

Ṣọpẹ́ Dìrísù Image Credit: WireImage On top of channeling an unmatched intensity in his performances, Dìrísù’s candidacy for the role of James Bond is largely derived from the actor’s breadth of experience working in the espionage genre. The British Nigerian actor began gaining recognition for his role as undercover detective Elliot Finch on the crime drama “Gangs of London,” resulting in his nomination for the Rising Star Award at the BAFTAs. But can Dìrísù pull off the nonchalance of Bond’s signature “ladies’ man”? The answer would prove to be yes, as seen through the actor’s embodiment of handsome bachelor Mr. Malcolm in the period piece “Mr. Malcolm’s List” — breeches and coattails never looked so good.

Nicholas Galitzine Image Credit: Getty Images After two breakout performances in 2023’s “Red, White & Royal Blue,” and “The Idea of You,” the baby-faced Britt proved he more than makes up for his youth with undeniable heartthrob potential. Galitzine lent his talents to another royally delicious drama in 2024, “Mary & George,” where he starred alongside Julianne Moore as her son George Villiers, tasked to gain influence over King James I by becoming his secret lover. More recently, his roles in “The Mosquito Bowl” and “Masters of the Universe” gave him a chance to switch genres. With a clear knack for seduction, Galitzine needs only a touch of action star training before becoming an ideal 007.

Kedar Williams-Stirling Image Credit: WireImage Williams-Stirling became a sex icon overnight with his break-out performance as misguided athlete Jackson Marchetti in Netflix’s “Sex Education,” but could the swoon-worthy actor swap Speedos for sky-blue Orlebar Brown trunks? The Manchester native has previously made appearances on other television series like action feature “Shank,” Shakespeare series “Will” and teen fantasy “Wolfblood” as well as lower-budget features like “Changeland,” but starring in the next Bond film would surely launch the Netflix star into high-profile feature roles.

Alfred Enoch Image Credit: Dave Benett/Getty Images for dun Hailing from notable franchises like “Harry Potter” and “How to Get Away with Murder,” British actor Alfred Enoch is a sleeper pick for the next 007. The actor’s warm smile can flash well during moments where Bond needs to work his charm to push his mission forward, while his physicality, which had notably been on display during a 2016 theater production of “King Lear,” can shine on full display when Bond needs to save the day. Enoch also had a recurring role on sci-fi series “Foundation,” and appeared in Anand Tucker’s thriller “The Critic.”

Fabien Frankel Image Credit: Getty Images Westeros hunk Fabien Frankel proved in “House of the Dragon” that he could handle the heat. The breakout star, who plays Dornish heartthrob Criston Cole, also impressed in “Task” and “The Serpent.” The actor has plenty of time ahead to fulfill the 15-year requirement. Plus, if he can wield a longsword, why not a PPK pistol?

article_text:
This week and next, Film Comment is reporting from the picturesque shores of the Lido, where the Venice Film Festival takes place each year. This year’s edition features new films by many major auteurs, including Werner Herzog, Lee Chang-dong, Tsai Ming-liang, and more.

For our second Podcast from the city of canals, critics Bilge Ebiri ( New York / Vulture ) and Guy Lodge ( Variety ) join Film Comment Co-Editor Devika Girish to discuss two standouts of the festival’s Competition section: Danny Boyle’s Ink (2:28) and Lee Chang-dong’s Possible Love (12:05). Next, they discuss a highlight of the Horizons sidebar: Robert Greene’s Too Much Sugar (27:30).

Subscribe to Film Comment to stay up-to-date with all of our Venice 2026 coverage.
excerpt_original: Bilge Ebiri and Guy Lodge share their reactions to Danny Boyle’s Ink , Lee Chang-dong’s Possible Love , and Robert Greene’s Too Much Sugar

article_text:
ジュディ・シル 贖罪のシンガーソングライター

劇場公開日： 2026年10月23日

映画館を探す

予告編を見る

映画チケットを U-NEXTでお得にゲット PR

解説・あらすじ

1970年代アメリカのフォークロック界で活動した孤高のシンガーソングライター、ジュディ・シルの知られざる人生と音楽に迫ったドキュメンタリー。 傑出した音楽的才能に恵まれながらも、その活動期には正当な評価を得られないまま、35歳で夭逝したジュディ・シル。1971年にデビッド・ゲフィンが設立したアサイラム・レコードの第1号アーティストとして、アルバム「ジュディ・シル」で華々しくデビューするも商業的には振るわず、徐々に音楽業界からフェードアウトしていった。 本作では、薬物中毒で荒れていた青春時代から、音楽界での活躍、そして悲劇的な死に至るまでの波乱万丈な人生を辿る。監督のブライアン・リンドストロームとアンディ・ブラウンが9年かけて集めたというシルの日記や楽譜、当時の記事、アーカイブ映像・写真など膨大な量の資料に加え、彼女の直筆の絵をアニメーション化することでその内面世界を表現。シルと同世代のミュージシャンであるジャクソン・ブラウン、グラハム・ナッシュ、ジュディから影響を受けたフリート・フォクシーズやビッグ・シーフらも登場し、彼女の音楽の魅力と人物像について、それぞれの視点から語る。製作総指揮には俳優のマヤ・ホークが名を連ねる。

2022年製作／91分／PG12／アメリカ 原題または英題：Lost Angel: The Genius of Judee Sill 配給：ディスクユニオン 劇場公開日：2026年10月23日

editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "《阿哥拉之爱》／香港白立方／2026年7月10日至8月29日／", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "一个鸟人；长着花瓣状光芒的独眼面孔；可当雨伞的真人大小蘑菇——大竹茂夫的超现实画作中反复出现一群奇异的混合角色与意象。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "其中一位身穿红裙的女孩，几乎出现在香港白立方《阿哥拉之爱》展出的每一件作品中。她有时从角落的门后探头张望，有时站在公共广场的市集入口前，有时站在大门前，或站在两只长满触角的生物之间——她总是停在某个界点上，穿行于两个实体之间无形的孔隙。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://i0.wp.com/artomity.art/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Shigeo-Otake-A-Little-Shopping-Trip-2026_1.jpg?resize=840%2C630&ssl=1", "alt": "", "caption": "大竹茂夫《小购物之旅》，木板蛋彩与油画，19 x 27.3 cm，21 x 29.3 x 4.5 cm（含框），2026年。© Shigeo Otake。摄影 © White Cube（Kitmin Lee）。", "credit": "Artomity", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在《阿哥拉之爱》中，大竹茂夫创造并探索了人类世界与异世界国度模糊时所产生的种种可能。他形容自己想象中的居民，是“不知怎么溜进我们世界的异界居民，以及发现自己身处另一个世界的普通人”。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "为了建立这个视角，艺术家需要一个代表普通人——也就是观者——的角色，于是构思了红裙女孩。她穿着经典制服，带着明显的天真与好奇，令人联想到儿童读物角色那种勇于冒险的精神：法国童书中的小女孩玛德琳，以及《爱丽丝梦游仙境》中的爱丽丝。“她也可能是我的投射。”大竹茂夫说。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这位艺术家以在神话与民间传说中加入个人特色的转化而闻名，将日本元素与西方、尤其是文艺复兴时期的技法结合，创作他的画作。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://i0.wp.com/artomity.art/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Shigeo-Otake-Skewer-Grill-Stall-2025_1.jpg?resize=840%2C630&ssl=1", "alt": "", "caption": "大竹茂夫《烤串摊》，木板蛋彩与油画，24.3 x 33.4 cm，26.3 x 35.5 x 4.5 cm（含框），2025年。© Shigeo Otake。摄影 © White Cube（Kitmin Lee）。", "credit": "Artomity", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "乍看之下，大竹茂夫精雕细琢的叙事构成令人联想到童书插画的画面。多重影响同时显现，例如漫画，以及通过他高度风格化的人物和他们似乎随时准备引发的混乱所体现的怪兽（巨大怪物在都市肆虐的电影类型）。他复杂的构图让人想起老彼得·布勒哲尔和希耶罗尼米斯·波希标志性作品中的无政府式狂乱，两人都经常描绘公共空间的大规模人群聚集与生活。然而，真正造就大竹茂夫独一无二美学的，是他对真菌的特殊迷恋，以及对寄生生物与虫草的研究——人类、动物与植物之间本应理所当然的社会阶序在此瓦解。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "大竹茂夫自称“昆虫男孩”，自小喜爱昆虫，也喜欢翻阅动植物图鉴和各类科学杂志，在阅读过程中逐渐认识了虫草。不过，他直到大学毕业成为画家后，才开始将真菌纳入自己的创作。他住在京都郊外一间共用的山边工作室时，曾偶遇一朵直径超过30厘米的大蘑菇，自此开始研究当地的真菌。他找到一本收录清水大辅详细插图的图鉴；清水大辅以营造融合写实与自然景观以及超自然奇幻世界的幻想风景艺术而闻名。“我当时尤其喜欢奇幻文学、推理小说和科幻小说，”大竹茂夫回忆道，“我希望观者能从熟悉的故事中，发现一种截然不同的表达方式。”", "这种细密程度反映了极其繁复的创作过程。就这件作品而言，除了使用他最偏爱的材料蛋彩画之外，大竹茂夫还采用了另一种由意大利文艺复兴画家发展出来的技法：揭取法（strappo），原本是为保存壁画而发展，用于将壁画从原有表面剥离并保存。大竹茂夫采用揭取法时，会先在墙面完成画作，再在表面覆上纱布；干透后轻轻将纱布剥下，贴到木板上，最后以水将纱布移除，让转移到木板上的画作自然风干。", "在这次旅行中，这位艺术家迷上了公共广场，并开始将它们用作自己许多画作的场景。“我也经常去市集，尤其是食品市集。那里会出售还带着头的动物尸体，或者一些我甚至无法想象该怎么吃的东西。总有一些令人惊讶的东西。我还觉得不同国家的市集差异如此之大，非常有趣。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "大竹茂夫的《菌市》（2026）描绘了公共广场上的露天市集，参照了法国艺术家巴尔蒂斯1933年的画作《街道》，反映出他对聚集与交换之场所的关注。各种交易与活动——无论寻常还是令人不寒而栗——都在这段叙事中展开。从明摆着出售各种货物，到前景中一个孩子在摊位底下偷女人的手提包，再到两名女子从窗户垂下的下半身，以及右后角一具似乎已经死亡的尸体被吊在空中，大竹茂夫和观者见证了一切，而那位红衣女孩正处在正中央的视野之中。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "大竹茂夫并非批判市集的交易本质，而是采取一种更具探究性和观察性的姿态。通过描绘交换的循环，他暗示了关于权力、金钱与日常生活相互关联的问题。因此，这些互动发生的公共空间，便成为大竹茂夫许多构图的理想场景。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", At times she’s peering from a doorway in a corner, placed at the entrance of a market in a public square, in front of a gate or between two tentacled creatures – always poised at a threshold, traversing the invisible porosity between two entities."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://i0.wp.com/artomity.art/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Shigeo-Otake-A-Little-Shopping-Trip-2026_1.jpg?resize=840%2C630&ssl=1", "alt": "", "caption": "A Little Shopping Trip by Shigeo Otake, Tempera and oil on board 19 x 27.3 cm,  21 x 29.3 x 4.5 cm (framed), 2026. © Shigeo Otake. Photo © White Cube (Kitmin Lee).", "credit": "Artomity"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "With Agoraphilia , Otake creates and explores the possibilities that arise when human and otherworldly realms blur, describing its imagined population as “inhabitants of another world who have somehow slipped into our own, and ordinary people who find themselves in the other world”."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "To forge this perspective, the artist needed a figure who represented an ordinary person – the viewer – and conceived the girl in red, whose classic uniform, apparent innocence and curiosity bring to mind the adventurous spirit of children’s-book characters: the French schoolgirl Madeline and Alice of Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland . “She may also be a projection of myself,” Otake says."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The artist is known for putting his own transformative twist on myths and folklore, combining Japanese influences with western, specifically Renaissance techniques to create his paintings."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://i0.wp.com/artomity.art/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Shigeo-Otake-Skewer-Grill-Stall-2025_1.jpg?resize=840%2C630&ssl=1", "alt": "", "caption": "Skewer Grill Stall by Shigeo Otake, Tempera and oil on board, 24.3 x 33.4 cm,  26.3 x 35.5 x 4.5 cm (framed), 2025. © Shigeo Otake. Photo © White Cube (Kitmin Lee).", "credit": "Artomity"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "At first glance, Otake’s intricately crafted narratives form visuals evocative of storybook illustrations. Numerous influences reveal themselves at once, such as manga and kaiju (the genre of films in which monstrous creatures wreak havoc on metropolises) through his highly stylised figures and the chaos they seem poised to inflict. His complex compositions bring to mind the anarchic frenzy present in Pieter Bruegel the Elder and Hieronymus Bosch’s iconic works, which often depicted large gatherings and life in public spaces. Yet it’s Otake’s niche fascination with fungi and his studies of parasitic life and cordyceps that yield a one-of-a-kind aesthetic – where the perceived social hierarchy of human, animal and vegetal beings collapses."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "A self-confessed “insect boy”, Otake has loved insects and enjoyed looking through illustrated books on plants and animals since childhood, as well as science magazines, where he developed a knowledge of cordyceps. However, it was after graduating from university and becoming a painter that he began incorporating fungi as a subject in his work. While staying in a shared mountainside studio on the outskirts of Kyoto, he encountered a large mushroom – over 30cm in diameter – prompting him to research local fungi. He came across a guide featuring the detailed illustrations of Daisuke Shimizu, best known for depicting fantasy landscape art that blends realism and natural scenery with fantastical, supernatural worlds. “I was especially fond of fantasy literature, detective and science fiction,” Otake recalls. “I would like viewers to be surprised by a different expression of a familiar story.”"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://i0.wp.com/artomity.art/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Shigeo-Otake-The-Magnate-2025_1.jpg?resize=840%2C630&ssl=1", "alt": "", "caption": "The Magnate by Shigeo Otake, Tempera and oil on board 24.3 x 33.4 cm, 26.3 x 35.5 x 4.5 cm,  (framed), 2025. © Shigeo Otake. Photo © White Cube (Kitmin Lee).", "credit": "Artomity"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Moments of drama and suspense live in the details of Otake’s vivid visuals, which is especially evident in works such as Phantom Realm Cafe (2026), where long-tongued, fish-like creatures peering from large shrubs in an outdoor cafe seem on the cusp of swallowing diners, waitstaff and their incoming orders in equal measure. In The Magnate (2026), amid what appears to be a potential roadside sale, a surreptitious figure in the corner can be stealing a small pouch hung from one of the wings of Otake’s hybrid bird-man icon."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Similar instances punctuate Night Parade of One Hundred Fungi (2026), a two-panel canvas that showcases the artist’s take on Hyakki Yagyō, a nighttime parade of supernatural beings famously depicted by Japanese painter and printmaker Kawanabe Kyōsai, often considered a pioneer of manga. Amid a carnivalesque atmosphere, Otake’s signature creatures – insects, marine life and human-fungal hybrids – lead a procession in front of shops that appear to be closed. All kinds of mushrooms sprout from every surface, from roofs to the tops of various heads."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://i0.wp.com/artomity.art/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Shigeo-Otake-Night-Parade-of-One-Hundred-Fungi-2026_1.jpg?resize=840%2C630&ssl=1", "alt": "", "caption": "Night Parade of One Hundred Fungi by Shigeo Otake, Strappo fresco mounted on board Overall: 72.7 x 181.8 cm, 2 parts, each: 72.7 x 90.9 x 2 cm, 74.7 x 184 x 4.5 cm (framed), 2026. © Shigeo Otake. "乍看之下，大竹茂夫精雕細琢的敘事令人聯想到童話書的插畫。作品以他高度風格化的人物，以及隨時準備引發的混亂，同時展現出多重影響，例如漫畫，以及描寫巨大怪物在都市肆虐的「怪獸」電影。他複雜的構圖讓人想起老彼得・布勒哲爾和希耶羅尼米斯・波希標誌性作品中的無政府式狂亂，兩人都經常描繪公共空間的大規模人群聚集與生活。然而，真正造就大竹茂夫獨一無二美學的，是他對真菌的特殊迷戀，以及對寄生之物與蟲草的研究，瓦解人類與動植物之間本應理所當然的社會階序。"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "大竹茂夫自稱「昆蟲男孩」，自小喜愛昆蟲，也喜歡翻閱動植物圖鑑和各類科學雜誌，在閱讀過程中逐漸認識了蟲草。不過他直到大學畢業成為畫家後，才開始將真菌納入自己的創作。他住在京都郊外一間共用的山邊工作室時，曾偶遇一朵直徑超過30厘米的大蘑菇，自此之後他便開始研究當地的真菌。他找到一本日本攝影師清水大輔的詳細圖鑑，清水大輔以營造融合寫實與自然景觀，以及超自然奇幻世界的幻想風景藝術聞名。大竹茂夫回憶道：「當時我尤其喜歡奇幻文學、推理小說和科幻小說。我希望參觀者能從熟悉的故事中，發現一種截然不同的表達方式。」"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "大竹茂夫鮮明畫面的細節中蘊藏著戲劇與懸念，這一點在《幻界咖啡館》（2026年）等作品中尤其明顯。戶外咖啡館的大型灌木叢後，幾隻伸出長舌的魚類生物探頭張望，彷彿下一刻就要把食客、侍應和送來的餐點一併吞下。在《大亨》（2026年）中，一幕看似路邊交易的場景裡，角落有個鬼鬼祟祟的身影，正從大竹茂夫筆下鳥人的其中一隻翅膀上偷走小袋子。"}, "paragraph", "text": "大竹茂夫在日本的藝術學校學習了不少藝術創作的西方元素，然而，大學最後一年在歐洲逗留的六個月，對他影響尤其深遠。"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在該次旅程中，藝術家開始迷上公共廣場，並逐漸將其作為許多畫作的場景。他表示：「我也經常去市集，尤其是食品市集，那裡會有連頭保留的動物肉殼出售，或者一些我無法想像可以吃的東西。那些市集總有令人驚訝的東西，我也覺得不同國家市集之間的差異非常有趣。」"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "大竹茂夫的《菌曜市》（2026年）描繪一個位於公共廣場的露天市集，取材自法國藝術家巴爾蒂斯1933年的畫作《街道》，反映出他對聚集與交流場所的迷戀。在這幅作品的敘事中，各種平凡和恐怖的交易與活動逐一展開。從陳列出售的各種商品，到前景在攤檔底偷女子手袋的孩童，到兩個從窗戶垂下的女子下半身，再到右後方角落一具被舉起的疑似屍體，所有都落入大竹茂夫與觀者的視線，而紅裙女孩正正站在畫面的中央前方，將這一切盡收眼底。"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "大竹茂夫並非要批判市集以交易為本的本質，而是採取一種更具探究性與觀察性的態度。透過描繪這種交換循環，暗示權力、金錢與日常生活彼此交織的問題。因此，發生這些互動的公共空間便成為了大竹茂夫許多構圖的理想場景。"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "他指出：「我真正想描繪的，是奇異生物與普通人接觸時所產生的戲劇性。市集正是一個特別引人入勝的相遇場景。」大竹茂夫捕捉這種互動的渴望，或最充分體現於《舊諏訪山動物園所見之幽靈》（2024年）。其中，長頸鹿、獵豹與雀鳥等動物被關在籠裡，而造物與人類則自由遊走，彼此互動，同時觀察籠內的動物。"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "真正令藝術家著迷的，是自然世界中相互依存的關係，這亦是他對真菌生命感興趣的根基，尤其是蘑菇如何與其他生物共存、與植物建立菌根關係、分解腐木，或寄生於昆蟲體內。他說自己很珍惜自然世界仍有許多未知：「我認為那個未知的領域是種寶貴的資源，我有一種強烈的迫切感，覺得在我們有機會認識和理解它之前，某些部分可能已因戰爭或環境破壞而消失。」"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "大竹茂夫創作的根基引出一個更根本的問題：我們如何找出一種與自然更平衡的共存方式，同時滿足人類無止境的消費慾望？或許那名身穿紅裙、站在界點上的女孩，正正在推動我們從旁觀走向參與，尋求一種更可持續的平衡。"}]

Agoraphilia / White Cube Hong Kong / Jul 10 – Aug 29, 2026 /

A bird-man; one-eyed faces sprouting petal-like rays; life-size mushrooms that function as umbrellas – Shigeo Otake’s surreal paintings feature a curious cast of recurring hybrid characters and motifs.

One in particular, a girl in a red dress, appears in almost all the works on view for Agoraphilia at White Cube Hong Kong. At times she’s peering from a doorway in a corner, placed at the entrance of a market in a public square, in front of a gate or between two tentacled creatures – always poised at a threshold, traversing the invisible porosity between two entities.

With Agoraphilia , Otake creates and explores the possibilities that arise when human and otherworldly realms blur, describing its imagined population as “inhabitants of another world who have somehow slipped into our own, and ordinary people who find themselves in the other world”.

To forge this perspective, the artist needed a figure who represented an ordinary person – the viewer – and conceived the girl in red, whose classic uniform, apparent innocence and curiosity bring to mind the adventurous spirit of children’s-book characters: the French schoolgirl Madeline and Alice of Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland . “She may also be a projection of myself,” Otake says.

The artist is known for putting his own transformative twist on myths and folklore, combining Japanese influences with western, specifically Renaissance techniques to create his paintings.

At first glance, Otake’s intricately crafted narratives form visuals evocative of storybook illustrations. Numerous influences reveal themselves at once, such as manga and kaiju (the genre of films in which monstrous creatures wreak havoc on metropolises) through his highly stylised figures and the chaos they seem poised to inflict. His complex compositions bring to mind the anarchic frenzy present in Pieter Bruegel the Elder and Hieronymus Bosch’s iconic works, which often depicted large gatherings and life in public spaces. Yet it’s Otake’s niche fascination with fungi and his studies of parasitic life and cordyceps that yield a one-of-a-kind aesthetic – where the perceived social hierarchy of human, animal and vegetal beings collapses.

A self-confessed “insect boy”, Otake has loved insects and enjoyed looking through illustrated books on plants and animals since childhood, as well as science magazines, where he developed a knowledge of cordyceps. However, it was after graduating from university and becoming a painter that he began incorporating fungi as a subject in his work. While staying in a shared mountainside studio on the outskirts of Kyoto, he encountered a large mushroom – over 30cm in diameter – prompting him to research local fungi. He came across a guide featuring the detailed illustrations of Daisuke Shimizu, best known for depicting fantasy landscape art that blends realism and natural scenery with fantastical, supernatural worlds. “I was especially fond of fantasy literature, detective and science fiction,” Otake recalls. “I would like viewers to be surprised by a different expression of a familiar story.”

Moments of drama and suspense live in the details of Otake’s vivid visuals, which is especially evident in works such as Phantom Realm Cafe (2026), where long-tongued, fish-like creatures peering from large shrubs in an outdoor cafe seem on the cusp of swallowing diners, waitstaff and their incoming orders in equal measure. In The Magnate (2026), amid what appears to be a potential roadside sale, a surreptitious figure in the corner can be stealing a small pouch hung from one of the wings of Otake’s hybrid bird-man icon.

Similar instances punctuate Night Parade of One Hundred Fungi (2026), a two-panel canvas that showcases the artist’s take on Hyakki Yagyō, a nighttime parade of supernatural beings famously depicted by Japanese painter and printmaker Kawanabe Kyōsai, often considered a pioneer of manga. Amid a carnivalesque atmosphere, Otake’s signature creatures – insects, marine life and human-fungal hybrids – lead a procession in front of shops that appear to be closed. All kinds of mushrooms sprout from every surface, from roofs to the tops of various heads.

The level of detail reflects an extremely laborious process. For this work specifically, in addition to using egg tempera, Otake’s preferred material, he employs another technique developed by Italian Renaissance painters: strappo , originally devised for preservation, to detach and maintain frescoes. Otake’s use of strappo includes completing the painting on a wall before applying gauze to the surface; once dry, the gauze is gently peeled away and applied to a wooden board, where the gauze is removed with water and the transposed painting left to dry.

While much of the western aspect of Otake’s artistic training was learned in art school in Japan, it was the six months he spent in Europe during his final year of university that were especially formative.

During this trip, the artist became fascinated with public squares and began using them as the setting for many of his paintings. “I also visited markets frequently, particularly food markets. There would be animal carcasses sold with their heads still attached or things that I could not even imagine how one might eat. There was always something surprising. I also found it fascinating how different the markets were from one country to another.”

Referencing French artist Balthus’s 1933 painting The Street , Otake’s Myco-Market (2026), depicting an open-air market in a public square, reflects his preoccupation with places of gathering and exchange. All manners of transaction and activity – both ordinary and chilling – unravel in this narrative. From the obvious display of various goods being sold to a child pickpocketing a woman’s handbag from underneath a stall in the foreground to the lower halves of two women hanging from windows and a seemingly dead body being hoisted in the air in the back right corner, Otake and the viewer are witness to all, vis-à-vis the girl in red who has a front-and-centre view.

Rather than critiquing the market’s transactional nature, Otake takes a more inquisitive and observational stance. By depicting the circle of exchange, he alludes to questions about the interconnectedness of power, money and everyday life. As such, public spaces where these interactions occur are optimal settings for many of Otake’s compositions.

“What I really want to depict is the kind of drama that arises when strange creatures and ordinary people come into contact with one another,” he says. “The marketplace is a particularly compelling setting for those encounters.” Otake’s desire to capture this interaction is perhaps most aptly realised in An Apparition Seen at the Former Suwayama Zoo (2024), where animals – giraffes, cheetahs and birds – are caged in captivity, while hybrid creatures and humans roam freely, interacting with each other and observing the animals.

It’s the natural world’s co-dependency that fascinates the artist, forming the foundation of his interest in fungal life – specifically how mushrooms live in relation to other organisms, forging mycorrhizal relationships with plants, decomposing dead wood or parasitising insects. He says that he values the fact that much is still unknown about the natural world. “I think that unknown realm is a precious resource. I feel a real sense of urgency about the possibility that parts of it may disappear through war or environmental destruction before we ever have the chance to know or understand it.”

The foundation of Otake’s work raises a more fundamental question – how do we find a more balanced way of living with nature that quenches humanity’s insatiable compulsion to consume? Perhaps the significance of the girl in the red dress standing at a threshold is to push us from observation to participation in achieving a more sustainable balance.

大竹茂夫的超現實畫作裡，反覆出現一群奇異的造物與意象：鳥人、綻放花瓣光芒的單眼面孔、可當雨傘的真人大小蘑菇。

其中一位身穿紅裙的女孩，幾乎在香港白立方「阿哥拉之愛」展覽的每一件作品中出現。她有時會從角落的門後探頭張望，有時會站在公共廣場的市集入口前，有時又會站在大門前，或站在兩隻長滿觸角的生物之間。她總是站在某個界點，穿梭於兩個實體之間無形的孔隙。

為了建立這個角度，藝術家需要一個代表普通人的角色，也就是觀者本身，於是他構思了紅裙女孩。她穿著經典的制服，帶著明顯的天真與好奇，令人聯想到兒童讀物角色那種勇於冒險的精神，像是法國童書中的小女孩瑪德琳，以及《愛麗絲夢遊仙境》中的愛麗絲。大竹茂夫說：「她也可能是我的投射。」

這位藝術家以在神話與民間傳說中加入個人特色而聞名，將日本元素與西方、尤其是文藝復興時期的技法結合，創作出他的畫作。

乍看之下，大竹茂夫精雕細琢的敘事令人聯想到童話書的插畫。作品以他高度風格化的人物，以及隨時準備引發的混亂，同時展現出多重影響，例如漫畫，以及描寫巨大怪物在都市肆虐的「怪獸」電影。他複雜的構圖讓人想起老彼得・布勒哲爾和希耶羅尼米斯・波希標誌性作品中的無政府式狂亂，兩人都經常描繪公共空間的大規模人群聚集與生活。然而，真正造就大竹茂夫獨一無二美學的，是他對真菌的特殊迷戀，以及對寄生之物與蟲草的研究，瓦解人類與動植物之間本應理所當然的社會階序。

大竹茂夫自稱「昆蟲男孩」，自小喜愛昆蟲，也喜歡翻閱動植物圖鑑和各類科學雜誌，在閱讀過程中逐漸認識了蟲草。不過他直到大學畢業成為畫家後，才開始將真菌納入自己的創作。他住在京都郊外一間共用的山邊工作室時，曾偶遇一朵直徑超過30厘米的大蘑菇，自此之後他便開始研究當地的真菌。他找到一本日本攝影師清水大輔的詳細圖鑑，清水大輔以營造融合寫實與自然景觀，以及超自然奇幻世界的幻想風景藝術聞名。大竹茂夫回憶道：「當時我尤其喜歡奇幻文學、推理小說和科幻小說。我希望參觀者能從熟悉的故事中，發現一種截然不同的表達方式。」

大竹茂夫鮮明畫面的細節中蘊藏著戲劇與懸念，這一點在《幻界咖啡館》（2026年）等作品中尤其明顯。戶外咖啡館的大型灌木叢後，幾隻伸出長舌的魚類生物探頭張望，彷彿下一刻就要把食客、侍應和送來的餐點一併吞下。在《大亨》（2026年）中，一幕看似路邊交易的場景裡，角落有個鬼鬼祟祟的身影，正從大竹茂夫筆下鳥人的其中一隻翅膀上偷走小袋子。

類似的情節也穿插於《百菌夜行》（2026年）之中，這幅雙聯畫布作品展現了藝術家對「百鬼夜行」的詮釋。「百鬼夜行」描述超自然生物於夜間遊行，因日本畫家及版畫家河鍋曉齋曾的描繪而馳名，他亦被視為漫畫先驅。大竹茂夫筆下的昆蟲、海洋生物，以及人類與真菌的混種等代表性生物在嘉年華氣氛籠罩下，於一排看似已關門的商店前列隊前行。各類蘑菇從所有表面冒出來，無論是屋頂到人物的頭頂都無處不在。

這種細密程度反映了極其繁複的創作過程。就這件作品而言，除了使用他最偏愛的材料蛋彩畫之外，大竹茂夫還採用了另一種由意大利文藝復興畫家發展出來的技法「揭取法」。這種技法原本是為了保存壁畫而發展，用於將壁畫從原有表面剝離並保存。大竹茂夫採用「揭取法」時，會先在牆面完成畫作，再在表面覆上紗布，乾透後輕輕將紗布剝下，再貼到木板上，最後以水將紗布移除，讓轉移到木板上的畫作自然風乾。

大竹茂夫在日本的藝術學校學習了不少藝術創作的西方元素，然而，大學最後一年在歐洲逗留的六個月，對他影響尤其深遠。

在該次旅程中，藝術家開始迷上公共廣場，並逐漸將其作為許多畫作的場景。他表示：「我也經常去市集，尤其是食品市集，那裡會有連頭保留的動物肉殼出售，或者一些我無法想像可以吃的東西。那些市集總有令人驚訝的東西，我也覺得不同國家市集之間的差異非常有趣。」

大竹茂夫的《菌曜市》（2026年）描繪一個位於公共廣場的露天市集，取材自法國藝術家巴爾蒂斯1933年的畫作《街道》，反映出他對聚集與交流場所的迷戀。在這幅作品的敘事中，各種平凡和恐怖的交易與活動逐一展開。從陳列出售的各種商品，到前景在攤檔底偷女子手袋的孩童，到兩個從窗戶垂下的女子下半身，再到右後方角落一具被舉起的疑似屍體，所有都落入大竹茂夫與觀者的視線，而紅裙女孩正正站在畫面的中央前方，將這一切盡收眼底。

大竹茂夫並非要批判市集以交易為本的本質，而是採取一種更具探究性與觀察性的態度。透過描繪這種交換循環，暗示權力、金錢與日常生活彼此交織的問題。因此，發生這些互動的公共空間便成為了大竹茂夫許多構圖的理想場景。

他指出：「我真正想描繪的，是奇異生物與普通人接觸時所產生的戲劇性。市集正是一個特別引人入勝的相遇場景。」大竹茂夫捕捉這種互動的渴望，或最充分體現於《舊諏訪山動物園所見之幽靈》（2024年）。其中，長頸鹿、獵豹與雀鳥等動物被關在籠裡，而造物與人類則自由遊走，彼此互動，同時觀察籠內的動物。

真正令藝術家著迷的，是自然世界中相互依存的關係，這亦是他對真菌生命感興趣的根基，尤其是蘑菇如何與其他生物共存、與植物建立菌根關係、分解腐木，或寄生於昆蟲體內。他說自己很珍惜自然世界仍有許多未知：「我認為那個未知的領域是種寶貴的資源，我有一種強烈的迫切感，覺得在我們有機會認識和理解它之前，某些部分可能已因戰爭或環境破壞而消失。」

大竹茂夫創作的根基引出一個更根本的問題：我們如何找出一種與自然更平衡的共存方式，同時滿足人類無止境的消費慾望？或許那名身穿紅裙、站在界點上的女孩，正正在推動我們從旁觀走向參與，尋求一種更可持續的平衡。

article_text:
This Ain’t About You

“This Ain’t About You” is an ongoing photographic project exploring everyday life in Geneva through the fleeting, often unnoticed moments that make up our daily existence.

The series focuses on small, everyday moments of people sharing the same streets. It is a way of being present in the city, rather than trying to explain it.

Geneva is both the setting and a silent participant in the work. A city often perceived through its polished, orderly and international image becomes something more human and unpredictable when observed through these fleeting encounters. The photographs are not intended to provide a definitive portrait of Geneva, but rather to capture the atmosphere of a place through the people who inhabit it.

The title “This Ain’t About” You is deliberately ambiguous. It refers both to the people photographed and to myself as the photographer. The images may appear to be about others, but they inevitably reveal something about the person observing, choosing and framing. In that sense, the project is also an exploration of the photographer’s own position within the world being photographed.

As part of this larger body of work, I recently produced a zine entitled Rive Gauche / Rive Droite. The zine can be seen as a window into the wider project, a self-contained fragment of a much larger photographic exploration of Geneva, its inhabitants and its everyday life.

article_text:
I n the early 1950s, Alvar Aalto built a boat to get to his remote summer residence on an island in Lake Päijänne, about 200km north of Helsinki . But the celebrated Finnish architect was not a happy skipper. He named the boat – a title as cumbersome as his buildings were elegant – Nemo propheta in patria: “No man is a prophet in his own land”.

The name was a dig at Finland , which the architectural maestro believed had taken him for granted. Other nations, he moaned, recognised his talent more than his own. Today, arriving in Helsinki, I find that Finland doesn’t just love Aalto, he’s a national treasure.

Last month, 13 Alvar sites dotted around Finland gained Unesco world heritage status. In addition to this international honour, vast quantities of Finnish public funding are being spent on the restoration of his buildings, and his designs are currently being celebrated in the Aalto Design – Shapes of Wellbeing exhibition at Helsinki’s Architecture & Design Museum. Norman Foster could but dream of such public adoration. For many Finns today, Aalto’s buildings – light-filled, harmonious habitats created from the mid-1920s to his death in 1976 – speak of national pride at a time of geopolitical tension with Russia and, further afield, connect to global considerations about “wellness” in the built environment.

But was it true that Aalto was once underappreciated at home? “The boat’s name wasn’t entirely in jest,” notes Sofia Nivarti, author of Studio Aalto, a new survey of his work to be published later this month. “The more he succeeded internationally, the more a local audience turned against him – steeped in a social-democratic ethos of egalitarianism, Finnish architectural circles worried about the dominance of one name over all others.”

In the first half of the 1950s, Aalto “wasn’t able to get a professorship from his alma mater, the Helsinki University of Technology,” explains Tommi Lindh, CEO of the Alvar Aalto Foundation. And a starchitect’s ego is a fragile thing, even in the cool egalitarian north.

In Helsinki, Lindh gives me a tour of the National Pensions Institute – now home to the Finns’ social security system – a vast brick building designed by Aalto between 1953 and 1957. It is perfectly preserved, right down to its ingenious overhead heating panels, angled skylights and working paternoster lift. This monumental brick building is one of five Aalto sites in Helsinki to gain Unesco recognition, alongside the House of Culture (commissioned by the Finnish Communist party in 1952, with the goal of “making culture the property of the entire nation”), Finlandia Hall, the vast, glacier-like concert and conference centre, and both Aalto’s home and his studio.

At the Shapes of Wellbeing exhibition, curators have broadened out the Aalto story to include the work of Alvar’s first wife, Aino, and second wife, Elissa, both skilled architects in their own right. It also shows that the experiential – and nature-loving – considerations Aalto brought to buildings also shaped his approach to furniture and lighting systems: his pendant lights recall beehives and jellyfish, his wooden chairs look as if they have been bent by the wind. “As we reconsider our relationship with nature and seek more sustainable ways of living, Aalto Studio’s work offers a valuable perspective,” says Pilvi Kalhama, director of the Architecture & Design Museum.

Naturally, Aalto’s domestic flourishes can also be found at his home in Munkkiniemi, Helsinki’s leafy, classy, equivalent of Hampstead. Completed in 1936, the Aalto House is a series of light-boxes overlooking a sports field, quiet but for birdsong and rippling with daylight. Aalto’s monochromatic abstract paintings still hang on the walls, his Homburg still sits in a wardrobe.

In contrast, Finlandia Hall – completed in 1971 and arguably his greatest masterpiece – introduces visitors to Aalto at his most symphonic. Standing in its concert hall – a jagged collection of white-on-white geometric planes – is like being inside an ice cube. A €136m renovation between 2022 and 2024 saw the building’s facade reclad in pristine Lasa Bianco Nuvolato marble and the opening of a permanent exhibition space dedicated to Aalto’s life and times.

Following Finland’s independence from Russia in 1917, the built environment – and Aalto’s mark on it – played a significant role in the shaping a new national identity. “Aalto did not set out simply to create a national style, but through his work he expressed values that became closely associated with modern Finland,” says Pilvi Kalhama. “Functionality, purpose, aesthetic quality and a progressive outlook were all central to his architecture and design. These qualities still reflect a broader Finnish attitude towards everyday life.”

As his compatriots once feared, Aalto’s international success has largely overshadowed the achievements of other Finnish architects. But these days, Finns seem less oppressed by his legacy. “You can’t really grow up as a Finnish architect without Aalto being part of your thinking. But that doesn’t mean we all want to design like him,” says Asmo Jaaksi, founding partner of JKMM Architects, which refurbished and restored Aalto’s House of Culture and has won the international competition to design a new Museum of Architecture and Design on Helsinki’s South Harbour (planned to open in 2030). “What I admire most is Aalto’s independence of thought, his willingness to experiment and his instinct for putting people and nature first. I think he’d be rather disappointed if we were all still copying him.”

At the height of Aalto’s career in the mid-20th century, he may have been sore at perceived slights, but his disgruntled state proved short-lived. “Aalto was a chameleonic persona,” says Sofia Nivarti. “Grumpy at times, yet bubbly and joyful to his core; moody and hilarious in turn; at times egotistical and at others deeply self-sacrificing and generous.” He was impossible to pigeonhole and his buildings embraced the contradictions of the human experience.

Soon enough, the Finns acknowledged his vision. In 1955, just as he launched his scornfully named boat, Aalto was elected as a member of the Finnish Academy. “He is the only architect in Finland to have received this position,” says Lindh. “Meaning the nemo propheta in patria days were over.”

Aalto Design – Shapes of Wellbeing is at the Architecture and Design Museum Helsinki until 3 January 2027. Studio Aalto by Sofia Nivarti is published by Yale University Press on 27 October 2026

article_text:
ホーム > 作品情報 > 映画「Blue Heron ブルーヘロン」

Blue Heron ブルーヘロン

劇場公開日： 2026年10月23日

解説・あらすじ

1990年代後半のカナダ・バンクーバー島を舞台に、8歳の少女の視点から家族と過ごしたかけがえのない日々をつづったヒューマンドラマ。 1990年代後半の夏。ハンガリー系移民の家族とともにバンクーバー島に移り住んだ8歳の少女サーシャは、豊かな自然に囲まれた土地で、兄たちや新しい友人と過ごしながら、少しずつ居場所を見つけていく。しかし、長兄ジェレミーは問題行動を繰り返しており、家族は限界を迎えそうになっていた。両親はジェレミーの問題を専門家に相談するなかで、困難な選択を迫られる。20年後、映画監督となったサーシャは、カメラを手に家族の過去をたどるなかで、幼い頃には見えなかった家族の姿を見つめ直していく。 監督・脚本は、本作が長編デビューとなるハンガリー系カナダ人の新鋭ソフィー・ロムバリ。これまでも「家族の記憶」「喪失」「写真や映像による記憶の再生」をテーマに短編作品を制作してきたロムバリ監督が、自身の家族との実体験をもとにフィクションとして再構築し、理解できない他者を見つめ続けることの尊さを描き出す。2025年・第50回トロント国際映画祭で最優秀カナダ映画新人賞を受賞したほか、世界各地で高く評価された。

バンクーバーの美しい風景とは裏腹に心がざわつく描写が多かったが、家族の温かみを感じられる場面もいくつかある。 ベートーヴェンの「皇帝」をBGMにした暗室のシーンが印象的だった。但しこのシーンは母親が不在なんだよね。 前半にアオサギの生態で「時が経つと群れの親密度がなくなる」みたいな説明があったけど、これって家族の暗喩なのかな。 そして20年後、専門家たちとの会議やジェレミーとの散歩での語らいなど、サーシャの空白を埋めていく凝った構成が斬新かつ見事だ。 全てを知る彼女の時空を超えた、両親へのアドバイスが哀しい。

2026年10月29日

iPhoneアプリから投稿

「わかり合えない」という悲しさと誠実に向き合う姿勢を、ドラマチックに解決させるのではなく、答えの出ない葛藤をそのまま見つめる誠実さに胸を打たれる。この世の理はこういうことのほうが多いのではないか。

2026年10月28日

iPhoneアプリから投稿

こういうタイプの作品とは相性があんまり良くないんですがチャレンジしてみました。 やっぱり相性は良くなかったんですが、予想していたベクトルとは違う相性の悪さでした。 問題行動の多い長男とどう向き合うかというのが根幹にあるとは思うんですが、どうしても反抗という言葉で済ませては良くないんじゃないかなというレベルの行動をしており、どうしてもなんかしらの障がいを抱えているんじゃないかなと最初の方から思っており、それを妹視点で見ながら進め、家族間の距離感も描くといった感じになっていました。 どうしても万引きを繰り返したり、自傷行為があったり、シンプルに人が嫌がることをするといった行動を咎めきれていないというのはやっぱり引っかかってしまいましたし、何を考えているのか、何をしたいのかというのが口数の少なさも相まって全然伝わってこない、汲み取るべきなんですが汲み取ってもなぁ…という感情にさせられるのは少し複雑でした。 時代は飛んで映画制作をしている妹の話があり、過去の体験談を映画に仕立てようと動く姿が映されるんですが、その話に繋がるんだという拍子抜け感とフィクションとノンフィクションが入り混じるかのような話運びがややこしさに拍車をかけていたなと思いました。 近い作品として「aftesun」が挙げられているみたいですが、あちらも苦手だったので系譜かなぁと。 中々好きになれないです、このドウヤァな感じ。 鑑賞日 10/26 鑑賞時間 15:30〜17:15

article_text:
Jenna Ortega opened up to Vogue magazine as part of a new cover story about her nonexistent relationship to how the public receives her movies. In other words, the “ Wednesday ” star does not watch her own movies or read reviews (because “that would send me into a psychosis of some sort’) or check the box office updates when her team sends them her way (because “I don’t want it to become a numbers thing”).

For most of her movie career, Ortega would rely on social media to gauge the chatter around her projects or to find out how much word of mouth existed around a certain project. But she’s even doing less of that these days since she’s on social media “less and less” because “so much of what you see on there nowadays is just garbage AI,” plus “we all look at ourselves too much.”

Ortega told Vogue that she recently broke her phone and didn’t even bother to get it fixed for a few days so she could be without social media and technology at her fingertips. She explained: “If I needed to get somewhere, if I had a workout class, I would look at a map on the computer, memorize the streets. If somebody needed me, I’m like, ‘Well, I’m gonna be at this café at this time.’ And that was so freeing.”

Ortega is gearing up for the release of her movie, the Taika Waititi-reviewed “ Klara and the Sun .” Reviews have not been kind to the movie, which is adapted from the Kazuo Ishiguro novel of the same name. Variety panned the film as “calamitous” and a “strained, whimsical comedy that’s ruinous.” The movie currently boasts a 27% on Rotten Tomatoes and is only tracking for a box office debut in the $2 million range despite a $20 million production budget. Fortunately for Ortega, she will stay clear of the reviews and the box office grosses.

In a separate interview on the “Happy Sad Confused” podcast , Ortega got more reflective about her television career. She currently headlines Netflix’s blockbuster series “Wednesday,” which is heading into its third season on the streamer. Ortega got her start on TV when she debuted at 9 years old on “Jane the Virgin” and went on to find Disney stardom on three seasons of “Stuck in the Middle.” Whenever “Wednesday” finally comes to an end, Ortega will be taking a TV break.

“What I’m meant to do will come and find me,” Ortega said. “I think after ‘Wednesday,’ I’ll probably be off the TV for a while. You know I had many years doing [TV]. I was bouncing from show to show as a kid and I want to leave time for new things.”

Read Ortega’s full Vogue cover story here . “Klara and the Sun” opens in theaters Oct. 23.

article_text:
AI meets YA head-on in the curiously flat comedy-drama Klara and the Sun , which almost perfectly illustrates how ill-prepared we are for the technological revolution that’s coming to us. In theory, Taiki Waititi should be a snug-as-a-bug fit for Kazuo Ishiguro ’s dystopian — or is it? — 2021 novel, given the director’s affinity for a very particular and peculiar kind of reality-based cringe comedy, but Klara just doesn’t deliver on any of the fronts it promises. Instead, we’re faced with a sporadically funny meditation on life and premature death that, like Mark Romanek’s gloomy attempt at Ishiguro’s 2005 novel Never Let Me Go , can’t quite capture the subtleties of speculative literary sci-fi.

If you hated Waititi’s 2019 film Jojo Rabbit , and the chances are inordinately high that you did, Klara and the Sun is pretty much that same film but in the future. But, contested as it is, Jojo Rabbit — like all of Waititi’s films — came from a good place, and what we have to determine now is whether he has drifted far off course or we have. What used to be so endearing, so naïve, and so vulnerable, just doesn’t work in this film, and the liminal space between films for kids and films for young-at-heart adults that he used to explore so incredibly well in his work — no better than in 2016’s Hunt for the Wilderpeople — now feels like an awkward no-man’s land between two very incompatible stories.

Watch on Deadline
