At least it starts with a spring in its step. Klara ( Jenna Ortega ) is a lonely pup in a robot shop, praying to the sun in the hope that she will be taken home by a passing punter (“Please let today be my day! Let me be chosen!”). Klara is a B1 robot on sale at The Friend Store, which is facing stiff competition from Fancy Friends over the road, where newer Bluetooth-active B3 models are taking over from the recently disgraced B2 models (“Is this the model that killed those people?” asks Klara’s potential buyer).

The Friend Store is a candy-colored prelude to what’s about to happen, with the wonderful Natasha Lyonne as The Store Manager, a den mother who loves her stock more than the outside world seems to. It’s hard to tell what year it is, but it’s clear that this is a future in which AI is evolving fast. But at the same time this is a future going backwards; The Store Manager talks wistfully about the internet, which was apparently taken away from everyone after the last world war (“You guys would have loved it”).

While posing artfully in the store’s shop window, Klara catches the eye of Josie (Mia Tharia), who persuades her mother Chrissie ( Amy Adams ) to buy her as a companion. The film is rife with theories as to why, in a city where bars have names like Ho Bots, people want artificial companions, and Klara’s immediate circle of friends are open to all options. One wants an owner who is sociable and popular (a jock); another wants someone who is needy and nerdy, with low self-esteem and “who thinks they are fat.”

Klara, though, lucks out with Josie, who, in a bid to raise the already elevated stakes, has been genetically “lifted” by a medical procedure that makes her a polymath. Josie lives in a remote country home with her not-very-attentive mother, but the real reason for Chrissie’s motives in acquiring a robot for her daughter is more than just buying her a friend: Josie is seriously ill. From here, the plot involves Klara finding out just how ill Josie is, and what she can do to save her, a journey that will take a very dark turn indeed.

At which point what’s left of the fun all but evaporates; Ortega is a fantastic cheerleader for the promised spirit of the film but, after she leaves Lyonne and the shop, all that is suddenly behind her; what lies ahead instead is the story of a mother who has already lost a daughter preparing to lose another. The possibilities of artificial life come into play much strongly here, notably with Steve Buscemi as the mysterious benefactor Capaldi, but, honestly, you’d have to be really quite thick not to see what’s coming.

Which is the problem throughout; everything about Klara and the Sun is face-palmingly obvious, particularly an excruciating scene in which Josie meets her new schoolmates, who listen to unlistenable avant-garde music, wear unwearable fashion-forward clothes and — are you ready for this? — lisp , as if the clothes and the music weren’t enough. It’s a weird moment that undermines everything the film has set in motion; for all its naivety, there’s a real push and pull here about the film’s intentions, and it isn’t a comfortable experience. The recent BBC series Ann Droid covered most of these ideas quite majestically, in an adult way that was also endearingly silly.

Similarly, on paper, Klara and the Sun is a great idea, a way for adults to explain mortality to their kids while bracing themselves for redundancy. It’s just a shame that film didn’t get made.

article_text:
With Uncool , her first book, fashion photographer Debora Brune, herself a wheelchair user, spent four years meeting and portraying models whose injured, ailing, or disabled bodies fall outside the norm.

By Guénola Pellen. Photos by Debora Brune.

Their disabilities are physical or sensory, present from birth or arriving with an accident or an illness. Fikayo’s blind eye is clouded a milky white. Beneath her hearing aid, Sophie has slipped a Vivienne Westwood earring, matched like a jewel. Caitlin has painted the toenails of her prosthetic leg with the same care as the rest. Lauren sits, sovereign, in her wheelchair. Scars, vitiligo, albinism, amputations: here, difference is shown without voyeurism and without pity.

Debora Brune came up through fashion before turning toward a more conceptual practice, probing the way bodies are seen, sorted, and made to behave. In 2026, she won the Dior Photography and Visual Arts Award at the Rencontres d’Arles. Her work, as Gui—who is albino and visually impaired—puts it, “captures individuals in their uniqueness, their beauty, and their abilities.” She does not soften what sets her subjects apart; she builds the beauty of the image around it. Natalie-Amber, a survivor of fulminant sepsis who now devotes her work to women everywhere, understood the gesture at once: “our body is our home, and we are beautiful just as we are.”

An ode to the sheer variety of bodies and their startling beauty, Uncool reveals the flesh with as much tenderness as nerve. Grace has worn a port-wine birthmark on the right side of her face since the day she was born. Catrin , burned across most of her body when a coach crashed in the Alps at nineteen, stands tall in a Burberry bikini. Debora Brune counts herself among her models, photographing her own back cleaved by a long white scar. These are bodies of pure presence. “My scars are a part of me, but they are not all of me,” Emma says. “To live with scarring on display can be terrifying, strong, upsetting, uplifting—but ultimately, it is part of you.”

Kjell is an actor. His drooping eyelid earned him a lifetime of people swearing he’d never make it in the business. He has learned not to give a damn. In the book he holds the camera’s eye, his gaze faintly veiled, his lips parted: “I no longer want to explain myself as a body.” J unior grew up in southeast London without ever once seeing a wheelchair user on television, in a schoolbook, or on the street. He went on to address the Houses of Parliament on the lack of workplace access and the way society looks at disability. “My existence shouldn’t make you uncomfortable. If I can find beauty and pride in myself and this world—so can you.”

Uncool by Debora Brune is self-published and available for €55.

Debora Brune will present the book and sign copies on Thursday, October 15, 2026, from 6 to 10 p.m. at the Open Space gallery in Berlin, Germany.

article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "No matter how one defines the films of the director Tinto Brass, who has died aged 93, they manage, in most cases, to keep a distance, however narrowly, from pornography. Although the Italian maestro of erotica never objected to being called a pornographer, he made the distinction by claiming: “I develop the moments of lust and desire out of the stories themselves .”", "links": [{"text": "the moments of lust and desire out of the stories themselves", "url": "https://www.evolver.at/reloaded/Tinto_Brass_Interview_2008/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "There is no doubt that most of his two dozen features, the most notorious being Salon Kitty (1976) and Caligula (1979) , could be variously labelled sexploitation (the female nude shown purely for sexual or commercial reasons), sexist, softcore (no erections or ejaculations), kitsch (bad taste) and camp (“its essence being its love of the unnatural: of artifice and exaggeration”, in Susan Sontag ’s definition).", "links": [{"text": "Caligula (1979)", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/film/2023/may/19/an-irresistible-mix-of-art-and-genitals-caligula-finally-comes-to-cannes"}, {"text": "Susan Sontag", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/news/2004/dec/29/guardianobituaries.booksobituaries"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "If a director who has a personal stamp, and whose oeuvre has a thematic and stylistic consistency, is considered an auteur, then Brass, who wrote and edited his own films, would qualify. Needless to say, he was in a different category from Federico Fellini , whom he idolised; Luchino Visconti, whom he parodied; and Roberto Rossellini , for whom he was assistant on two films. Yet, in the early 1960s, Brass was thought of as one of the most interesting directors of the new generation.", "links": [{"text": "Federico Fellini", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/theguardian/2013/nov/01/federico-fellini-dies-film-italy"}, {"text": "Roberto Rossellini", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/film/2025/oct/24/i-told-him-i-had-secretly-seen-his-films-his-eyes-filled-with-tears-isabella-rossellini-remembers-her-father-roberto"}]}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/6520576bd30c017e3b8ae845dd2eb38f2573a2d5/0_0_4252_2836/master/4252.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none", "alt": "Malcolm McDowell as Caligula and Helen Mirren as his wife, Caesonia, in Caligula (1979).", "caption": "Malcolm McDowell as Caligula and Helen Mirren as his wife, Caesonia, in Caligula (1979). Photograph: Collection Christophel/Alamy", "credit": "The Guardian · Culture"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "He had met Jean-Luc Godard , François Truffaut and others in Paris, and assisted Henri Langlois, the eccentric chief of the Cinémathèque Française in Paris, on a short documentary on the artist Marc Chagall. For his first feature, To the Ends of the Earth (1963), Brass paid homage to Ermanno Olmi ’s Il Posto (1961) – both films are about a young man’s first job in a large, dehumanising office – as well as to Godard’s Vivre Sa Vie (1962), by casting Sady Rebbot, who played a murderous pimp in the earlier film, in the lead.", "links": [{"text": "Jean-Luc Godard", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/film/2022/sep/13/jean-luc-godard-obituary"}, {"text": "Ermanno Olmi", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/film/2018/may/07/ermanno-olmi-obituary"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Although Italian, the film had a French new wave feeling about it. Unfortunately, the censors objected to a certain anti-Catholicism and demanded cuts. Brass refused, and the film stayed on the shelf for a number of years."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Born in Milan but brought up in Venice, he was the son of Carla Curletti and Alessandro Brass, a lawyer. His grandfather, the Venetian painter Italico Brass, encouraged his grandson Giovanni’s artistic leanings and nicknamed him “Tintoretto”, later shortened to Tinto. After studying law at the universities of Padua and Ferrara, graduating in 1957, he went to the Cinémathèque Française, and on his return to Italy worked for Rossellini.", "links": [{"text": "Italy", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/world/italy"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Brass entered commercial cinema by directing two episodes of the omnibus comedy My Wife (1964), starring Silvana Mangano and Alberto Sordi , and a spaghetti western, Yankee (1966), which he tried to make as close as possible to Sergio Leone’s hit films with Clint Eastwood, many similar stylistic devices.", "links": [{"text": "Alberto Sordi", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/news/2003/feb/27/guardianobituaries2"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "A move to swinging London resulted in four weird psychedelic films: Deadly Sweet (1967), a thriller starring Jean-Louis Trintignant ; Nerosubianco (1969), an inter-racial romance; The Howl (1970), a freewheeling pop cultural fantasy; and Dropout (also 1970) with the real-life lovers Vanessa Redgrave and Franco Nero. The couple also starred, with Corin Redgrave , in Vacation (1971), a mixture of medieval and modern fable.", "links": [{"text": "Jean-Louis Trintignant", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/film/2022/jun/17/jean-louis-trintignant-obituary"}, {"text": "Corin Redgrave", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/stage/2010/apr/06/corin-redgrave-obituary"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Then, in 1972, the now controversial Deep Throat, the first pornographic picture to be shown in mainstream cinemas, where it made an estimated $600m, opened the way for Brass to abandon eclecticism and start a new career. “Out of the blue, one could get a big budget and sponsorship deals for explicit material. Photograph: Moviestore Collection/Alamy", "credit": "The Guardian · Culture"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Salon Kitty, which starred Helmut Berger as a power-mad SS officer (a reference to Visconti’s The Damned, 1969), is a decadent tale in which young women are trained to entertain Nazi officers in a high-class brothel in Berlin in 1939. The protagonists celebrate and, in full knowledge of impending doom, the excesses become increasingly bizarre.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Ostensibly, Caligula was also about the depravity of excessive power, as conceived by Gore Vidal in his earlier screenplay, before the Penthouse magazine publisher Bob Guccione , who co-produced, decided that it did not plumb the depths demanded and added extra scenes (written and directed by Guccione) and recut others to provide more titillation.", "links": [{"text": "Gore Vidal", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/books/2012/aug/01/gore-vidal-dies"}, {"text": "Bob Guccione", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/culture/2010/oct/21/bob-guccione-obituary"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "As a result, Caligula, with a prestigious cast including Peter O’Toole , John Gielgud, Helen Mirren and Malcolm McDowell (in the title role), became nothing more than toga-dropping soft porn. Both Brass and Vidal demanded that their names be stricken from the credits. Ironically, it remains the film with which Brass is most associated.", "links": [{"text": "Peter O’Toole", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/film/2013/dec/15/peter-o-toole-dies-81"}, {"text": "John Gielgud,", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/film/2000/may/22/news.obituaries"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "In 2010, Brass announced that he was to “revisit an abandoned project about a Roman emperor that was ruined by Americans”, in 3D. That never came to pass, but in 2023 Caligula: The Ultimate Cut emerged. Running 178 minutes (just over 20 minutes longer than the original), it was pieced together by the art historian Thomas Negovan from 96 hours of raw footage. Gone was the Guccione material; Negovan instead used alternate takes from the archives to create a version of the film closer to Vidal’s original script.", "links": [{"text": "Caligula: The Ultimate Cut", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/film/article/2024/aug/07/caligula-the-ultimate-cut-review-ambitious-1979-shocker-minus-the-spurious-porn"}, {"text": "Thomas Negovan", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/film/2023/may/19/an-irresistible-mix-of-art-and-genitals-caligula-finally-comes-to-cannes"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Important elements were brought to the fore; Mirren, on screen for no more than 20 minutes as Caligula’s wife, Caesonia, in the 1979 cut, now had an hour of screen time, while the range and texture of McDowell’s performance was made newly vivid. “McDowell doesn’t exactly earn the audience’s sympathy,” said Variety magazine, “but the actor charts the young man’s path from ambitious successor to maniacal despot with much greater clarity and believability than ever before.”"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/9f4029b37aa31b2367615b68010b25ca2ba307c1/0_0_4252_2836/master/4252.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none", "alt": "In a scene from Caligula, a woman in teal raises her arms before a man on an ornate bed", "caption": "Despite the prestigious cast, Caligula was ‘nothing more than toga-dropping soft porn’. Photograph: TCD/Prod DB/Alamy", "credit": "The Guardian · Culture"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Many reviewers expressed surprise at the partial and miraculous rehabilitation of this notorious folly. On its first release, Caligula had come in for a critical battering. The US critic Roger Ebert found it “sickening, utterly worthless, shameful trash.", "links": [{"text": "Roger Ebert", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/film/2013/apr/04/roger-ebert"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "If it is not the worst film I have ever seen, that makes it all the more shameful. People with talent allowed themselves to participate in this travesty … Caligula is not good art, it is not good cinema, and it is not good porn.” Nevertheless, despite the negative reviews, the movie went on to make a lot of money and, inevitably, become a cult favourite, a status that Brass’s subsequent raunchy romps were not bad enough to achieve."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Among his classier and more restrained ones was The Key (1983), starring Stefania Sandrelli with Frank Finlay as her ageing husband. Set in Venice at the time of Mussolini’s rise to power, it had lush settings and a catchy Ennio Morricone score.", "links": [{"text": "Frank Finlay", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/stage/2016/jan/31/frank-finlay"}, {"text": "Ennio Morricone", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/music/2020/jul/06/ennio-morricone-obituary"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Miranda (1985) was the first of several erotic comedies that were on the frontier of hardcore. article_text:
No matter how one defines the films of the director Tinto Brass, who has died aged 93, they manage, in most cases, to keep a distance, however narrowly, from pornography. Although the Italian maestro of erotica never objected to being called a pornographer, he made the distinction by claiming: “I develop the moments of lust and desire out of the stories themselves .”

There is no doubt that most of his two dozen features, the most notorious being Salon Kitty (1976) and Caligula (1979) , could be variously labelled sexploitation (the female nude shown purely for sexual or commercial reasons), sexist, softcore (no erections or ejaculations), kitsch (bad taste) and camp (“its essence being its love of the unnatural: of artifice and exaggeration”, in Susan Sontag ’s definition).

If a director who has a personal stamp, and whose oeuvre has a thematic and stylistic consistency, is considered an auteur, then Brass, who wrote and edited his own films, would qualify. Needless to say, he was in a different category from Federico Fellini , whom he idolised; Luchino Visconti, whom he parodied; and Roberto Rossellini , for whom he was assistant on two films. Yet, in the early 1960s, Brass was thought of as one of the most interesting directors of the new generation.

He had met Jean-Luc Godard , François Truffaut and others in Paris, and assisted Henri Langlois, the eccentric chief of the Cinémathèque Française in Paris, on a short documentary on the artist Marc Chagall. For his first feature, To the Ends of the Earth (1963), Brass paid homage to Ermanno Olmi ’s Il Posto (1961) – both films are about a young man’s first job in a large, dehumanising office – as well as to Godard’s Vivre Sa Vie (1962), by casting Sady Rebbot, who played a murderous pimp in the earlier film, in the lead.

Although Italian, the film had a French new wave feeling about it. Unfortunately, the censors objected to a certain anti-Catholicism and demanded cuts. Brass refused, and the film stayed on the shelf for a number of years.

Born in Milan but brought up in Venice, he was the son of Carla Curletti and Alessandro Brass, a lawyer. His grandfather, the Venetian painter Italico Brass, encouraged his grandson Giovanni’s artistic leanings and nicknamed him “Tintoretto”, later shortened to Tinto. After studying law at the universities of Padua and Ferrara, graduating in 1957, he went to the Cinémathèque Française, and on his return to Italy worked for Rossellini.

Brass entered commercial cinema by directing two episodes of the omnibus comedy My Wife (1964), starring Silvana Mangano and Alberto Sordi , and a spaghetti western, Yankee (1966), which he tried to make as close as possible to Sergio Leone’s hit films with Clint Eastwood, many similar stylistic devices.

A move to swinging London resulted in four weird psychedelic films: Deadly Sweet (1967), a thriller starring Jean-Louis Trintignant ; Nerosubianco (1969), an inter-racial romance; The Howl (1970), a freewheeling pop cultural fantasy; and Dropout (also 1970) with the real-life lovers Vanessa Redgrave and Franco Nero. The couple also starred, with Corin Redgrave , in Vacation (1971), a mixture of medieval and modern fable.

Then, in 1972, the now controversial Deep Throat, the first pornographic picture to be shown in mainstream cinemas, where it made an estimated $600m, opened the way for Brass to abandon eclecticism and start a new career. “Out of the blue, one could get a big budget and sponsorship deals for explicit material. That helped me immensely,” he explained. “Salon Kitty would have otherwise never been made, at least not in that form.”

Salon Kitty, which starred Helmut Berger as a power-mad SS officer (a reference to Visconti’s The Damned, 1969), is a decadent tale in which young women are trained to entertain Nazi officers in a high-class brothel in Berlin in 1939. A mix of graphic sex, arty production design (by Ken Adam of James Bond films fame), and heavy political statements, the film was more honest than other nasty Nazi exploitation films it spawned.

“To me, the point is to stage the dance on the figurative volcano,” Brass explained. “Because that’s exactly what happens when power reaches its zenith. The protagonists celebrate and, in full knowledge of impending doom, the excesses become increasingly bizarre.”

Ostensibly, Caligula was also about the depravity of excessive power, as conceived by Gore Vidal in his earlier screenplay, before the Penthouse magazine publisher Bob Guccione , who co-produced, decided that it did not plumb the depths demanded and added extra scenes (written and directed by Guccione) and recut others to provide more titillation.

As a result, Caligula, with a prestigious cast including Peter O’Toole , John Gielgud, Helen Mirren and Malcolm McDowell (in the title role), became nothing more than toga-dropping soft porn. Both Brass and Vidal demanded that their names be stricken from the credits. Ironically, it remains the film with which Brass is most associated.

In 2010, Brass announced that he was to “revisit an abandoned project about a Roman emperor that was ruined by Americans”, in 3D. That never came to pass, but in 2023 Caligula: The Ultimate Cut emerged. Running 178 minutes (just over 20 minutes longer than the original), it was pieced together by the art historian Thomas Negovan from 96 hours of raw footage. Gone was the Guccione material; Negovan instead used alternate takes from the archives to create a version of the film closer to Vidal’s original script.

Important elements were brought to the fore; Mirren, on screen for no more than 20 minutes as Caligula’s wife, Caesonia, in the 1979 cut, now had an hour of screen time, while the range and texture of McDowell’s performance was made newly vivid. “McDowell doesn’t exactly earn the audience’s sympathy,” said Variety magazine, “but the actor charts the young man’s path from ambitious successor to maniacal despot with much greater clarity and believability than ever before.”

Many reviewers expressed surprise at the partial and miraculous rehabilitation of this notorious folly. On its first release, Caligula had come in for a critical battering. The US critic Roger Ebert found it “sickening, utterly worthless, shameful trash.

If it is not the worst film I have ever seen, that makes it all the more shameful. People with talent allowed themselves to participate in this travesty … Caligula is not good art, it is not good cinema, and it is not good porn.” Nevertheless, despite the negative reviews, the movie went on to make a lot of money and, inevitably, become a cult favourite, a status that Brass’s subsequent raunchy romps were not bad enough to achieve.

Among his classier and more restrained ones was The Key (1983), starring Stefania Sandrelli with Frank Finlay as her ageing husband. Set in Venice at the time of Mussolini’s rise to power, it had lush settings and a catchy Ennio Morricone score.

Miranda (1985) was the first of several erotic comedies that were on the frontier of hardcore. Based on a Carlo Goldoni play, it featured Serena Grandi as a tavern owner deciding which of three men she will settle down with. With titles such as Così Fan Tutte (All Ladies Do It, 1992), The Voyeur (1994), Frivolous Lola (1998), Cheeky (2000) and Black Angel (AKA Senso ’45, 2002), an updated remake of Visconti’s Senso (1954), Brass continued to find a specific, mostly male, audience.

Brass’s first wife, Carla Cipriani, a writer and assistant director, whom he married in 1957, died in 2006. He is survived by their son, Bonifacio, and daughter, Beatrice, and by his second wife, the actor Caterina Varzi, whom he married in 2017.

Tinto Brass (Giovanni Brass), film director, screenwriter and editor, born 26 March 1933; died 4 November 2026

article_text:
AMC Theatres CEO Adam Aron has issued an open letter to New York City residents reiterating the company’s desire to continue operating its longstanding Kips Bay 15 multiplex in the Manhattan neighborhood of that name, but concedes the decision is not AMC’s to make.

Neighbors of the Kips Bay-Murray Hill section of Manhattan along Second Avenue near the East River have been vocal about the planned closure of the multiplex that’s been a central commercial hub since 1999 (AMC took over the venue in 2006). The property on which the multiplex sits was privately purchased last year by NYU Langone, one of New York’s major health care systems.

Related Stories

AFM Partners With AMC Century City To Expand Theatrical Screenings For Sales Companies, Producers

Kyle Davies Exits Bleecker Street For AMC Theatres' New Distribution Label Leawood Films

AMC announced in August that the purchase would likely mean the closure of the multiplex by the end of this year, prompting an outcry and protests from residents and other businesses in the area.

Watch on Deadline

Following “direct engagement” from Manhattan Borough President Brad Hoylman-Sigal, AMC’s Aron issued the open letter concurring with Hoylman-Sigal that the neighborhood needs such amenities as a movie theater, supermarket and housing.

Writes Aron, “Since news first broke that our popular AMC Kips Bay 15-screen movie theatre located at 570 Second Avenue in Manhattan will soon be forced against our will to close its doors, I’ve been struck by the extraordinary support that this AMC theatre has received from within the local surrounding community.”

Read the entire statement below.

“AMC Theatres does not want to go,” Aron writes. “Not one little bit. AMC Theatres wants to stay in Kips Bay….Apparently, NYU Langone Health does not share that view, not ours or not yours. Unfortunately, the decision to retain or end AMC’s tenure in Kips Bay is not ours to make.”

According to Aron, the NYU Langone Health facility “wants to expand, seems to be in the process of buying the building in which your (our) theatre now operates, and it wants us gone. In anticipation of such a transfer to NYU Langone, the current building’s owner has terminated our lease.”

Aron notes that AMC has “engaged” with NYU Langone to suggest various alternatives that would allow the multiplex to continue operating in some form. “Sadly, any and all variations that we have proposed have fallen on closed minds,” he writes, adding, “We call on NYU Langone Health to open their minds, to think creatively, and come up with a solution that will give the Kips Bay community BOTH of the two things that is wanted most of all: expanded facilities offering the world class medical care that is the hallmark of NYU Langone Health AND a fully functional AMC Theatre on Second Avenue.”

The AMC chief warns that time is running out for the venue. “Unless NYU Langone Health lets us delight the Kips Bay community beyond then, to comply with our terminated lease, the lights on AMC Kips Bay 15 will forevermore see their final sunset on January 3, a mere two and a half months from now.”

AMC currently operates nine multiplexes in Manhattan.

Check out this week’s selections below and past round-ups here .", "links": [{"text": "here", "url": "https://thefilmstage.com/tag/new-to-streaming"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Bad Apples (Jonatan Entzler)"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://thefilmstage.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/10/Bad-Apples.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "The Film Stage"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "To international viewers, Bad Apples will play like a conventional dark comedy about a schoolteacher pushed too far by a student; to Brits, it’s a scorched Earth takedown of a state education system that has failed millions of children, any laughs to be had cathartic through the tears. What’s surprising is that such a state-of-the-nation takedown arrives courtesy of Swedish director Jonatan Entzler in his English-language debut, relocating Scandinavian source material to a classroom in the southwest of England. article_text:
Each week we highlight the noteworthy titles that have recently hit streaming platforms in the United States. Check out this week’s selections below and past round-ups here .

Bad Apples (Jonatan Entzler)

To international viewers, Bad Apples will play like a conventional dark comedy about a schoolteacher pushed too far by a student; to Brits, it’s a scorched Earth takedown of a state education system that has failed millions of children, any laughs to be had cathartic through the tears. What’s surprising is that such a state-of-the-nation takedown arrives courtesy of Swedish director Jonatan Entzler in his English-language debut, relocating Scandinavian source material to a classroom in the southwest of England. Working with breakthrough screenwriter Jess O’Kane, he’s done an impeccable job encapsulating decades of political failures towards younger generations into a morally slippery kidnapping comedy, weaponizing viewers’ own experiences in the classroom (both as parents and students) to try making you empathize with the criminal adult over their victim. It’s provocative simply because it’s a crowd-pleaser that relies on you abandoning any shred of empathy, highlighting a societal problem by making unsuspecting viewers delight in the worst possible solution to it while revealing unconscious biases. – Alistair R. ( full review )

Where to Stream: VOD

Carolina Caroline (Adam Carter Rehmeier)

How do you tell when you stop being good people pretending to be bad and realize you’re just bad people who can’t even trick themselves into thinking they’re anything but? Caroline (Samara Weaving) asks this aloud earlier than you might expect, considering the crime escapade she and new boyfriend Oliver (Kyle Gallner) enjoy commenced at her behest. She didn’t just take his advice and wonder why she’d never left the one place she’s ever known. She didn’t just reject the notion of staying because it’s safe. No, Caroline chose to meet those realities with the decision to become a full-blown outlaw because it made her feel truly alive. – Jared M. ( full review )

Where to Stream: Netflix

Do You Love Me (Lana Daher)

In what could’ve also been called Lebanon Plays Itself , Lana Daher’s ambitious, all-archival Do You Love Me captures some 70 years of Lebanese history, curated from a search that began with more than 20,000 potential sources . Consolidated to just 76 minutes, the resulting feat of montage is an experiment as playful as it is informative, showing a country in turmoil and citizens who still find happiness in everyday life. – Jordan R.

Where to Stream: VOD

Drunken Noodles (Lucio Castro)

The laws of time and space are met with frisky ambivalence in Drunken Noodles , Lucio Castro’s anticipated third feature and surely the hottest title in this year’s ACID lineup. Most people familiar with the New York-based, Argentinian-born director first encountered him through End of the Century, a film of similar temporal disregard: set in Barcelona, it followed two men who seemed to fall in love only to realize it wasn’t their first encounter. Upon release in 2019, critics were divided over some of the film’s more adventurous flourishes––the sense of overreach. There are a handful of moments in Noodles that do something similar, but it’s an otherwise sultry and strangely calming film, 82 minutes of late-night hookups and late-season ennui that passes like a summer breeze. – Rory O. ( full review )

Where to Stream: The Criterion Channel

The History of Concrete (John Wilson)

Like a movie tie-in, John Wilson’s debut documentary feature, The History of Concrete , picks up immediately where his HBO series How To with John Wilson left off after three seasons. An elevated public profile does not lead to the next bigger, better project. Instead it’s illustrated via Wilson stumbling upon an empty bag of weed featuring an unauthorized branding of his likeness. The full-sized crew afforded by his show now absent, Wilson is forced back to his roots, filming the day-to-day scenes of New York City life solo. – Caleb H. ( full review )

Where to Stream: VOD

Making Marie Antoinette (Eleanor Coppola)

Wrapped inside the visual splendor, luxurious elegance, and ornate decoration of Sofia Coppola’s resplendent and anachronistic Marie Antoinette is the story of a young woman leaving her family behind to help lead another country—an unknown journey and simultaneous document of wealth, excess, and its depressive isolation. Yet despite Coppola tapping into her short filmography’s recurring themes, at least on set, she never contended with the same separation and loneliness of her ill-fated heroine. That’s largely because her mother, Eleanor Coppola, was always by her side—lurking and observing and recording 80 hours of behind-the-scenes footage with her digital camera inside the halls of Versailles. – Jake K-S. ( full review )

Where to Stream: MUBI

Musk (Alex Gibney)

A dense, probing, ultimately terrifying exploration of the world’s richest man, Alex Gibney’s four-hour opus Musk isn’t going to reveal anything new about the CEO of Tesla and SpaceX that you couldn’t glean from the myriad books, podcasts, and articles. There’s no smoking gun to explain his laser-like focus on domination or even his intense rightward political shift in recent years. Yet in sweeping across Musk’s life since about 1995—when he founded his first company, Zip2—Gibney nevertheless paints a damning picture in its totality and simplicity. That’s because for all his talk of AI, self-driving cars, and colonizing Mars, Elon Musk is a frighteningly simple person to decipher. The illusion of wealth, status, and brilliance that he carried through the 1990s finally gave way to actual wealth and status by hustling and grifting his way into a succession of companies that were already marginally successful. – Christian G. ( full review )

Where to Stream: VOD

Nicolas Cage

One of the most iconic cinematic presences is getting a well-deserved spotlight on the Criterion Channel this month, featuring Fast Times at Ridgemont High , Rumble Fish , Valley Girl , Birdy , Peggy Sue Got Married , Moonstruck , Raising Arizona , Vampire’s Kiss , Wild at Heart , Leaving Las Vegas , City of Angels , Snake Eyes , Bringing Out the Dead , Adaptation , Matchstick Men , The Wicker Man , and Bad Lieutenant: Port of Call New Orleans .

Where to Stream: The Criterion Channel

Possible Love (Lee Chang-dong)

In a year of unknown quantities at the Venice Film Festival, Lee Chang-dong’s Possible Love has delivered the triumph for which fans of the elusive director had been hoping. Lee’s first feature since Burning , a modern masterpiece that blew away the competition in Cannes eight years ago, is another novelistic gem, the kind of richly detailed and intricately scripted yarn in which alluring themes like class, sex, and sociology are always on the table to be picked at. It also bears a much-wider and more-specific political purview than its predecessor, which comes at a cost for its dramatic pull from time to time. Lee’s nevertheless returned with the most substantial film I’ve seen in this year’s competition and one that is easily amongst the best of the year so far. – Rory O. ( full review )

Where to Stream: Netflix ( Note: Netflix has also added most of Lee’s other films, including his 2022 short Heartbeat , available online for the first time ever)

Primetime (Lance Oppenheim)

Robert Pattinson was born to play Chris Hansen. In the opening shot of Lance Oppenheim’s Primetime —the documentary savant’s first foray into fiction, this one based on a true story—we immediately see the popular To Catch a Predator host as the menace Oppenheim and first-time screenwriter Ajon Singh want us to understand him as. He’s cast in a devilish red light, swallowed by shadow, displayed through an eerie mini-DV grain, and reciting the lines “I will undress you and you will undress me” over and over in Hansen’s trademark brassy, rehearsed, does-he-really-sound-like-that (yes, he does) tone. The chilling music of the haunted fairytale score glitches in and out while children’s-show chimes ring ominously. – Luke H. ( full review )

Where to Stream: VOD

Resident Evil (Zach Cregger)

Resident Evil , as a game series, has always borrowed heavily from cinema, whether it be the fixed angles and Kiyoshi Kurosawa inspirations of the first title to the Texas Chainsaw riffs in the 7th. It’s less about the zombies, more the feeling of powerlessness and weird puzzles. Zach Cregger understands this on a deep level. His follow-up to Weapons may not be a pitch-perfect adaptation of the long-running lore, but it perfectly captures the spirit of Resident Evil as a whole, not to mention what it’s like to play it. The perfect title might actually have been Biohazard . – Devan S. ( full review )

Where to Stream: VOD

Sense and Sensibility (Georgia Oakley)

It’s always tempting to discuss Jane Austen adaptations in comparison with their predecessors, especially when the most famous example here is Ang Lee’s version that earned Emma Thompson her second Oscar. Georgia Oakley recognizes this; rather than trying to reinvent the wheel or subvert this text, she instead delivers a sublime take that more than justifies returning to the well once more. For as much as we desire original stories, there’s just as much pleasure to be taken from a solid translation of sturdy material. And it confirms the Blue Jean director as a major talent—a great eye who can put a definite stamp on outside sources without going overboard. – Devan S. ( full review )

Where to Stream: VOD

Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother (Bassam Tariq)

Latif (Mahershala Ali) is a righteous man. A religious man. He sees himself in a holy war to cleanse the world of his people’s enemies by picking up where the law ends. Those who know about his work justifiably condemn it, whether that be his Imam (Giancarlo Esposito’s Abdul Malik) or his wife. They don’t, however, condemn him . Because they understand his struggle. They know his pain. Why add to it? So, they grant him mercy instead. They accept him and hope he will one day find his way back. – Jared M. ( full review )

Where to Stream: VOD

article_text:
Martin Scorsese ‘s “ Cleopatra ” never came to fruition, and he says the Angelina Jolie -starrer was nixed because of Seth Rogen and the Sony hack.

For those who need a refresher, Sony emails were hacked in November 2014 by a group that hoped the Seth Rogen comedy “The Interview,” which was about a fictional assassination attempt of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, would not be released by Sony.

Related Stories

Ethan Klein Reacts to Hila Klein's Cheating Allegations Amid 'H3 Podcast' Fallout: 'Please Respect My Family's Privacy ... They Have Nothing to Do With This'

H3 Podcast Crew Cuts Ties With Ethan Klein After Hila Klein Says He Has Been Having an Affair

According to Scorsese, this caused some aftereffects in the industry, which he described in the first episode of the Tribeca original series “ Crafty .”

“We were gonna do Cleopatra at one point, and then they made fun of [Kim Jong Un], and he got mad and blew up everybody at Columbia,” Scorsese said. “Seth Rogen, right? And then he got mad, and [it] ruined Cleopatra.”

Though Rogen wasn’t directly responsible for the project being canceled, the resulting hack exposed thousands of emails, including ones from producer Scott Rudin to Sony’s Amy Pascal calling Jolie “a minimally talented spoiled brat.”

“We were gonna do it,” Scorsese also said. “Angelina Jolie. We were going. She was gonna be Cleopatra VII. It was gonna be really wild.”

The film was set to be written by screenwriter Eric Roth, who wrote Scorsese’s 2023 film “Killers of the Flower Moon.”

Watch the episode of “Crafty” below.

article_text:
民主党が上下両院を奪還、ホワイトハウスの舞踏室建設はどうなる？ トランプ大統領は続行の構え

約4億ドル（約630億円）を投じるとされるホワイトハウスの舞踏室建設計画は、中間選挙で民主党が上下両院の過半数を奪還したことで、先行きが不透明になっている。それでも トランプ大統領 は、選挙翌日の11月4日に行われた式典で、建設への意欲を改めて示した。

11月3日に投開票が行われたアメリカの中間選挙で、民主党は連邦議会の上下両院で過半数を奪還した。しかし、 ドナルド・トランプ 大統領は選挙結果を気にする様子を見せず、約4億ドル（約630億円）をかけてホワイトハウスにボールルーム（舞踏室）を新設する計画への意欲を改めて示した。

ボールルームの建設計画は、用地確保のためにホワイトハウスのイースト・ウィングを取り壊したことに加え、地下に軍事施設を併設すると表明したことから、当初から物議を 醸してきた 。また、大統領が議会の承認なしに大規模な建設計画を進める権限を持つのかという問題も浮上し、連邦裁判所で計画の適法性が 争われてきた 。

民主党が2027年1月に上下両院の主導権を握ることで、建設計画が予定どおり進められるかどうかは依然として不透明だ。この計画をめぐっては、歴史的建造物の保護に取り組む非営利団体、全米歴史保存財団（National Trust for Historic Preservation）が建設の差し止めを求める訴訟を起こし、連邦地裁と控訴裁が地上部分の工事差し止めを認めていた。しかし、最高裁は8月31日、同団体に訴訟を起こす資格が認められない可能性が高いとして、差し止め命令の効力を 停止した 。これにより工事の続行が可能となったが、計画そのものの適法性については判断を示していない。

こうした状況のなか、トランプ大統領は11月4日に行われた、ボールルームの最後の鉄骨を取り付ける式典で、完成後の建物について 次のように語った 。

「これは特別な建物です。世界最大級というだけでなく、世界で最も美しいボールルームになると思います」

また、ホワイトハウスの改修に時間を費やしているという批判に対しては、次のように反論した。

「なぜ私がホワイトハウスの改装に時間を費やしているのか、選挙期間中にも少し話題になりました。ですが、実際にはほとんど時間をかけていません。それに、私はこういうことが好きなんです。楽しいですし、私にとっては気分転換にもなります」

（翻訳：編集部）

世界最古の老人ホーム跡が見つかったヒッポス国立公園の遺跡。Photo: Courtesy of Dr. Michael Eisenberg

14.古代都市遺跡から「世界最古の老人ホーム」跡──1600年前の高齢者の生活を示す貴重な発見 イスラエル・ハイファ大学の研究チームによる古代都市ヒッポスの発掘調査で見つかった施設跡が、世界最古の老人ホームである可能性が高いと8月18日に発表された。【続きを読む】 Photo: Courtesy of Dr. Michael Eisenberg

13. モーセが実在した証拠か──3800年前の碑文の新解釈が物議。手がかりは高解像度写真と3Dスキャン 旧約聖書の『出エジプト記』に登場し、十戒や海割りで知られるモーセの実在性について、現在では歴史的事実の裏付けはないとされることが一般的だ。しかし、それをくつがえす新説を唱える学者が現れた。【続きを読む】 Photo: De Agostini via Getty Images

12. 古代エジプト彫刻の常識を覆す発見！ 墓荒らしが見逃した石像がサッカラ遺跡で出土 エジプトのサッカラ遺跡で、盗掘者が放置した石像が発見された。丸彫りと浮き彫りを併用したこの石像は、古王国時代に類例のない作品として、専門家たちの関心を呼んでいる。【続きを読む】 Photo: Courtesy of Zahi Hawass Library

男性の後ろ脚に隠れる姿て彫られている少女。Photo: Courtesy of Zahi Hawass Library

8. 3000年前のマヤ文明遺跡群を発見。先コロンブス期の社会政治的・宗教的構造への理解を深める手がかりに グアテマラ北部でマヤ文明の遺跡群が発掘された。3つの都市遺跡にまたがる約16平方キロの地域で、約3000年前のピラミッドや聖域、独自の運河システムなどが見つかっている。【続きを読む】Photo: Courtesy the Guatemalan Ministry of Culture and Sports

6. ポンペイの家族を襲った悲劇が明らかに。ドアをベッドで封鎖し最期まで抵抗を試みる 79年8月、ヴェスヴィオ火山の噴火による火砕流に襲われた古代都市ポンペイ。突然の災害から最期の瞬間まで生き延びようと試みた1つの家族の物語が新しい調査で明らかになった。【続きを読む】 Photo: Courtesy Pompeii Archaeological Park

5. メキシコの密林に古代都市を発見！ 要塞の「真の姿」がレーザー測量によって明らかに カナダのマギル大学の研究者が実施したレーザー測量調査によって、これまで要塞だと考えられてきたメキシコの密林地帯に古代都市が眠っていることが明らかになった。【続きを読む】 Photo: Pedro Guillermo Ramón Celis, and the Guiengola Archaeological Project

都市の中心地。ピラミッドや寺院などが多く建てられている。Photo: Pedro Guillermo Ramón Celis, and the Guiengola Archaeological Project

東側に位置していた居住エリア。Photo: Pedro Guillermo Ramón Celis, and the Guiengola Archaeological Project

Photo: Pedro Guillermo Ramón Celis, and the Guiengola Archaeological Project

4. 約1300年前の黄金の釈迦如来レリーフをタイの涅槃像下で発見。金・銀・青銅の遺物が多数出土 タイ東北部の由緒ある寺院で涅槃仏の保存活動を行っていたところ、黄金の釈迦如来坐像のレリーフなど、約1300年前のものと見られる貴重な遺物が多数発見された。【続きを読む】 Photo: Courtesy Thailand Fine Arts Department

article_text:
Feature

Gochman Collection Builds a Home for Native Art in Westchester

The private collection opened its Branchline location in Katonah as a way to bring Native art into public view, though questions linger about its engagement with the local Lenape community.

Line Break on November 5 (all photos Petala Ironcloud/

Hyperallergic , unless otherwise noted)

KATONAH, NY — In 1680, English colonists bought the land that would become Bedford, New York, from a Munsee Lenape sachem named Katonah , meaning “great hill.” Today, his name belongs to a Westchester village that is now home to Branchline, the Gochman Family Collection’s (GFC) new gallery and studio space, which opened to the public on November 6 with Line Break , an exhibition of works drawn primarily from its holdings of contemporary Native American art.

Since its founding in 2021, GFC has collected over 800 works with support from Native and non-Native gallerists, artists, and curators alike, including Creative Director and Curator Rachel Martin (Tlingít), curator and Hyperallergic contributor Shándíín Brown (Diné), and Director Laura Phipps, who also serves as Branchline’s director. Designed by Elizabeth Roberts Architects, the new space occupies two historic storefronts steps from Katonah’s Metro-North station, with free-admission galleries, skylit artist studios, a community ceramics studio, and apartments for invited artists.

Branchline makes a public home for what has essentially been a lending operation: According to GFC, more than 260 of its works have appeared in over 100 exhibitions at institutions including the Metropolitan Museum of Art, the Whitney Museum of American Art, and The Broad, and it charges no loan fees. That model speaks to a known problem with private collecting, explained Joseph Pierce (Cherokee), professor and founding director of the Native American and Indigenous Studies Initiative at Stony Brook University. “Just because you collect something doesn’t mean you’re going to show it,” Pierce told Hyperallergic . “The risk is that it doesn’t circulate.”
